a-living-night-sky-underground-the-waito.context_blurb: The Waitomo Caves are a long limestone cave system on the North Island of New Zealand. Clinging to the ceilings of some of its chambers are enormous colonies of glowworms — the bioluminescent larvae of a small fungus gnat found almost nowhere else — which produce faint blue-green points of light as a lure for insect prey. Boat tours drift through pitch-dark grottoes under a 'living night sky' of thousands of these tiny lights. The caves have been shown to visitors by the local Maori family who own them since the 1880s.

a-volcano-is-born-new-land-in-a-human-li.context_blurb: Most of the Earth's volcanoes have been in roughly the same places for thousands of years. But every so often, a brand-new volcano is born in a place where there was no volcano before. In 1943 one appeared in a Mexican cornfield (Paricutin) and over the next nine years grew into a 400-metre cone. In 1963 another erupted up out of the sea off Iceland (Surtsey) and became a new island. These rare, well-documented events give geologists a chance to watch, in real time, the birth of a volcano from scratch.

abu-simbel.context_blurb: Abu Simbel is a pair of enormous rock-cut temples in the far south of Egypt, near the border with Sudan. They were ordered by Pharaoh Ramesses II in the 13th century BCE as a lasting statement of his glory, their fronts guarded by colossal seated statues of the pharaoh himself. In the 1960s, when the Aswan High Dam was built and the rising lake of its reservoir was going to drown the temples, an international team of engineers performed one of the most audacious rescues in archaeological history to save them.

ajanta-caves.context_blurb: The Ajanta Caves in central India are a horseshoe-shaped line of about thirty Buddhist monasteries and chapels carved directly into a sheer cliff above a river, in two bursts of work spanning the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. Their interiors are decorated with some of the oldest and most beautiful surviving paintings in all of Indian art, depicting the life of the Buddha and tales of his previous existences. The caves were abandoned, grown over by jungle, and completely forgotten for over a thousand years until a British officer stumbled on them in 1819.

akrotiri-and-the-thera-eruption-santorin.context_blurb: The Greek island of Santorini (ancient Thera) in the Aegean Sea is actually the shattered rim of a volcano, standing in a ring around a drowned central basin. In roughly 1600 BCE Thera erupted in one of the biggest volcanic explosions of the last ten thousand years, blowing out its own middle. Buried on the island is the Bronze Age Minoan town of Akrotiri, preserved under metres of ash in a state so good that houses still stand two storeys high. Its wall-paintings are among the most beautiful anywhere in the ancient world.

aksum.context_blurb: Aksum, in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, was the capital of one of the great African empires of antiquity. From about the 1st to the 7th centuries CE it controlled the Red Sea trade and became, in the 4th century, one of the earliest kingdoms anywhere to adopt Christianity as its official religion. Its site is still a sacred city for the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, and ancient tradition holds that one of the holiest objects of the Hebrew Bible rests inside a guarded chapel there.

alexandria.context_blurb: Alexandria, on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, was founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BCE and became the capital of Hellenistic Egypt under Alexander's general Ptolemy and his descendants. It was for several centuries the biggest and most sophisticated Greek-speaking city on Earth — the home of a famous library, a famous lighthouse (one of the ancient Seven Wonders), and a cosmopolitan mix of Greek, Egyptian, and Jewish scholars. Much of the ancient city now lies underwater offshore, drowned by earthquakes and the slow subsidence of its coast.

amritsar-the-golden-temple-in-its-sacred.context_blurb: Amritsar, in the Indian state of Punjab, is the holiest city of the Sikh religion. In its very centre sits a shining temple whose upper storeys are gilded and whose base is reflected in a square pool of sacred water, from which the city takes its name ('pool of nectar'). Sikhism, founded in the 15th century, teaches the equality of all people before one God; the temple is approached by a long causeway and welcomes visitors from any faith. Every day its community kitchen serves a free meal to tens of thousands of pilgrims regardless of class or creed.

amsterdam-the-city-on-piles-below-the-se.context_blurb: Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands, built on soft swampy ground in the delta where the Rhine, the Meuse, and the Scheldt all meet the North Sea. Much of it sits below sea level and would be underwater without an extraordinary system of dams, dykes, and pumps that the Dutch have been building and refining for centuries. The old city of concentric canals was laid out in the 17th century, the 'Dutch Golden Age,' when a tiny country briefly ran one of the richest trading empires on Earth.

angel-falls.context_blurb: Angel Falls, in southeastern Venezuela, is the tallest uninterrupted waterfall in the world — a single straight drop of water nearly a kilometre long. It pours over the sheer sandstone edge of a flat-topped table mountain, or tepui, in the middle of a remote jungle so inaccessible that it can mostly only be reached by small plane and dugout canoe. It is named after the American aviator Jimmie Angel, who crash-landed on top of the tepui in 1933 and whose stories brought the falls to international attention.

angkor-siem-reap.context_blurb: Angkor is the ruined medieval capital of the Khmer Empire, in modern Cambodia near the small modern town of Siem Reap. From roughly the 9th to the 15th centuries it was the heart of a Hindu-Buddhist empire that controlled much of Southeast Asia, and at its height Angkor was the largest preindustrial city in the world. The jungle swallowed it after it was abandoned, until French archaeologists in the 19th century began cutting back the vines. Dozens of temples are scattered across its plain.

angkor-thom-and-the-bayon.context_blurb: Angkor Thom was the fortified royal capital built in the late 12th century by King Jayavarman VII of the Khmer Empire, inside the great complex of Angkor in modern Cambodia. In its exact centre stands the Bayon temple, famous for its 54 towers each sculpted with giant stone faces, serene and half-smiling, gazing out in every direction. The whole square city is surrounded by a moat and five grand gates, each approached by a causeway lined with gods and demons churning a cosmic ocean.

angkor-wat.context_blurb: Angkor Wat, in modern Cambodia, is the largest religious building on Earth. It was built in the first half of the 12th century by King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire as a vast temple-mountain to the Hindu god Vishnu, surrounded by a square moat so wide that its outer edge is more than a kilometre on a side. Later generations converted it to Buddhist use. For about four hundred years it was the heart of a city grander than any in medieval Europe, until the court moved on; monks have never stopped tending it since.

antarctica.context_blurb: Antarctica is the continent at the bottom of the world, almost entirely covered by an ice sheet up to several kilometres thick. It is the coldest, driest, and windiest continent, and no humans live there permanently — only scientists on rotating tours of duty at a few dozen research stations. Antarctica was discovered only in the 19th century. Under the 1959 Antarctic Treaty, no country owns the continent; it is reserved for peaceful scientific cooperation, and all territorial claims are frozen.

antarctica-the-windiest-coldest-place-on.context_blurb: Antarctica is the coldest and windiest continent on Earth. Its interior plateau regularly records air temperatures below -80 degrees Celsius, lower than any other place on the planet, and gale-force winds funnel down from the ice sheet to the coasts almost every day. The Antarctic ice sheet is so cold and so dry that paleoclimate records drilled out of it go back more than 800,000 years. A handful of research stations host rotating teams of scientists, but there are no cities, no indigenous people, and no permanent human residents.

atalh-y-k.context_blurb: Chatalhoyuk, in central Turkey, is one of the earliest 'cities' ever discovered — a dense cluster of mud-brick houses first built around 7500 BCE, more than four thousand years before Stonehenge was begun. It had no streets. The houses were packed wall-to-wall, so that people walked on the rooftops and entered their homes from above through holes in the ceiling. Its wall-paintings include what may be the world's oldest known landscape picture and the oldest surviving map.

athens.context_blurb: Athens is the capital of Greece and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth. In the 5th century BCE, during a brief and dazzling period, it was the home of democracy's first flowering, of the historian Thucydides and the dramatists Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, of the philosophers Socrates and Plato, and of some of the greatest buildings ever raised in white marble, perched on a rocky citadel in the middle of the city.

auckland.context_blurb: Auckland is the largest city in New Zealand, built on a narrow isthmus between two harbours on North Island. The surrounding landscape is studded with the small volcanic cones of a young volcanic field that has produced dozens of eruptions over the last quarter-million years. The whole field is still considered active. Despite being New Zealand's biggest city, Auckland is not its capital; that honour goes to Wellington further south.

ayutthaya.context_blurb: Ayutthaya was for over four hundred years the capital of the Siamese kingdom that eventually became Thailand. It stood on a river island in the central Thai plain, and in the 17th century it was described by European visitors as rivalling Paris or London in size and grandeur. In 1767 a Burmese army took it, sacked it, and burned it down. The capital was moved south to Bangkok and Ayutthaya was never rebuilt. Its red-brick stupas and broken Buddha statues still stand in the ruined city as an evocative sprawl of temples.

baalbek.context_blurb: In the Beqaa Valley of modern Lebanon stands Baalbek, where the Romans built one of the largest temple complexes anywhere in their empire. Dedicated chiefly to Jupiter, its surviving columns are among the tallest ever raised in the ancient world. What really baffles visitors, though, is the platform the temples stand on: a few of its foundation stones are so monstrously heavy — hundreds of tonnes each — that modern engineers still argue over exactly how the Romans quarried and moved them.

babylon-and-the-ishtar-gate.context_blurb: Babylon was for many centuries the greatest city of Mesopotamia, in the floodplain of modern Iraq. Under King Nebuchadnezzar II in the 6th century BCE it was rebuilt in dazzling blue-glazed brick, with a ziggurat tower, hanging gardens that may or may not have existed, and a famous processional entrance called the Ishtar Gate, lined with striding animals in relief. A large reconstructed section of that gate is now one of the great treasures of a European museum.

bagan.context_blurb: On a bend of the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar lies the Bagan plain, the religious capital of a medieval Burmese kingdom. Over about two and a half centuries, from the 11th to the 13th, the kings of Bagan and their devoted subjects raised thousands of Buddhist temples, stupas, and pagodas across its dry grassland. Many have crumbled; many still stand. Watching dawn mist rise over a plain prickled with so many brick spires is one of the most unearthly sights in Buddhist Asia.

baghdad.context_blurb: Baghdad was founded in 762 CE on the banks of the Tigris River in modern Iraq by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur, as the fresh capital of the vast Muslim Abbasid Empire. For a few golden centuries it was the richest and most learned city on Earth, home of the 'House of Wisdom' where scholars translated and extended the mathematics and medicine of the ancient Greeks, Persians, and Indians. In 1258 the Mongols sacked the city so completely that it never fully recovered its former glory.

bali-uluwatu-and-the-subak.context_blurb: Bali, a small island at the eastern end of Java in Indonesia, is unusual: in a mostly Muslim country, it remains overwhelmingly Hindu, with its own distinctive form of Balinese Hindu religion and culture. The island's dramatic cliff-edge sea-temples look out over the Indian Ocean. Inland, its hillsides are terraced into intricate step-pools of flooded rice fields that are irrigated by an ancient cooperative water-management system called the Subak, which Balinese farmers have run as both a hydraulic and a religious institution for over a thousand years.

bangkok.context_blurb: Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, grew from a riverside village into a sprawling metropolis of around ten million people, built on and around the delta where the Chao Phraya River meets the Gulf of Thailand. The old city centre is a tight warren of temples, markets, and canals; the newer city is a lattice of skyscrapers, elevated roads, and shopping malls. Its official ceremonial name, used in school textbooks, is one of the longest city names in the world. It is slowly sinking into its soft delta mud.

barcelona-gaud-s-growing-basilica.context_blurb: Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia on the Mediterranean coast of Spain. Its architecture is dominated by the strange, swooping, organic designs of Antoni Gaudi, a devout Catalan architect of the late 19th and early 20th centuries who built houses, parks, and churches that look like they have grown out of the sea or the forest. His great unfinished basilica — begun in 1882, still rising from scaffolding, and only now approaching completion — is one of the most singular buildings ever conceived.

batik-javas-wax-drawn-cloth.context_blurb: Batik is the Indonesian art of dyeing patterns onto cloth by first drawing them in liquid wax. Wherever the wax goes, dye cannot reach, so when the wax is boiled off the design remains in the natural colour of the fabric. The island of Java is its traditional home, and Javanese batik is extraordinarily elaborate: a single piece might take months of work, with multiple layers of waxing, dyeing, and re-waxing to build up complex multi-coloured patterns. UNESCO has recognized Indonesian batik as part of the world's cultural heritage.

beijing-the-imperial-capital.context_blurb: Beijing has been the capital of China for most of the last seven centuries, under the Yuan, Ming, Qing, and modern governments. In its exact middle stands the Forbidden City, the vast walled palace from which emperors ruled a quarter of humanity and into which ordinary subjects were not permitted to set foot. The city was laid out according to classical cosmological principles, with its main axis running north-south through gate after gate and courtyard after courtyard. Modern Beijing has sprawled far beyond it, but the imperial geometry is still visible from the air.

bergen.context_blurb: Bergen is on the fjord-indented west coast of Norway, surrounded on three sides by mountains and the open sea on the fourth. In the Middle Ages it was Norway's largest city and the main northern outpost of the Hanseatic League, the trading alliance that dominated commerce around the Baltic and North Sea. Its old wooden warehouse-wharf — Bryggen — is still lined with narrow painted buildings from that era. Bergen sits in the path of nearly every Atlantic storm, which is why it is one of the rainiest cities in Europe.

bodh-gayas-bodhi-tree-and-the-traveling-.context_blurb: Bodh Gaya, in the eastern Indian state of Bihar, is the single holiest site in Buddhism. According to tradition, it is the place where in the 5th century BCE a wandering ascetic named Siddhartha Gautama sat under a tree and attained enlightenment, becoming the Buddha. The tree now standing at the site is itself a descendant of the original. A tall ornately decorated brick temple, the Mahabodhi, marks the spot. Monks and pilgrims from Buddhist countries all over Asia come here throughout the year.

borobudur.context_blurb: On the volcanic island of Java in Indonesia stands Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument in the world. It is a mountain-shaped stepped pyramid of grey volcanic stone, built in the 9th century CE, and pilgrims walk a long clockwise spiral path up through terraces carved with hundreds of relief panels depicting Buddhist teachings. The whole temple was overwhelmed by volcanic ash and jungle for centuries and only restored in the 20th century, in one of the largest archaeological rescues ever undertaken.

brasilia.context_blurb: Brasilia is the capital of Brazil, and it was carved out of empty highland savanna in the middle of the country in just a few years at the end of the 1950s. President Juscelino Kubitschek wanted a modern capital to pull Brazil's centre of gravity inland from the crowded coast. The architect Oscar Niemeyer and the planner Lucio Costa laid out a brand-new city of sweeping concrete curves and modernist buildings, finished in 1960. From the air it has an unmistakable, deliberate silhouette.

bruges-the-port-that-froze-in-time.context_blurb: Bruges, in Belgium, was in the Middle Ages one of the richest trading cities of northern Europe — one of the first homes of modern banking, and the headquarters of some of the earliest great painters of the Flemish school. Then its connection to the sea silted up and the trade moved on, leaving the city in a long, poor sleep. Because it was too hard-up to tear itself down and rebuild, its medieval and Renaissance centre has survived almost intact, with cobbled lanes, canals, bell-towers, and gabled houses.

bryce-canyon.context_blurb: Bryce Canyon, in southern Utah in the United States, is not really a canyon at all; it is a cluster of natural amphitheatres eroded into the eastern edge of a high plateau. The amphitheatres are packed with thousands of thin, tall, often orange-and-pink spires of rock, called hoodoos. They are produced by freeze-and-thaw erosion acting on alternating layers of hard and soft limestone. One early Mormon settler was reportedly asked what he thought of the strange landscape and answered that it was a hell of a place to lose a cow.

budapest.context_blurb: Budapest is the capital of Hungary, split by the Danube River into two halves — hilly, old Buda on the west bank and flat, bustling Pest on the east. The two were only merged into a single city in 1873. The city sits on top of a system of hot springs, and its grand bath-houses (some built by the Ottomans, some by the Hungarians themselves) have been in continuous use for centuries. It is also one of the great architectural cities of Central Europe, from medieval Buda Castle to the enormous neo-Gothic parliament on the riverbank.

buenos-aires.context_blurb: Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina, sits on the muddy estuary where the Parana and Uruguay rivers run into the Atlantic. It was flooded by waves of European immigration between the 1870s and 1930s — mostly Italian and Spanish — which left the city with grand belle-epoque boulevards nicknamed 'the Paris of the Americas.' Its culture is distinct within Latin America: Spanish accented with an Italian lilt, strong coffee, late dinners, and a passionate home-grown dance born in its port-side neighborhoods at the end of the 19th century.

bukhara-the-silk-road-museum-city.context_blurb: Bukhara, in modern Uzbekistan, was for a thousand years one of the great cities of the Silk Road, where overland caravans between China, India, Persia, and Europe passed through. It was a famous centre of Islamic scholarship — the great medieval physician Ibn Sina (Avicenna) was from near here — and later became the capital of a line of khans. Mongol invaders, Timurid emperors, and Soviet planners all left marks on it. Its medieval centre of brick madrasas, minarets, and domed markets is extraordinarily well preserved.

byblos-and-the-phoenician-alphabet-that-.context_blurb: Byblos, on the coast of modern Lebanon, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world. In the Bronze Age it was a Phoenician port, and it was Phoenician traders who developed and spread, around 1050 BCE, a radically new way of writing: a short alphabet in which each sign stood for a single consonant sound rather than a whole word or syllable. As Phoenician merchants sailed around the Mediterranean, their script was adopted and adapted by Greeks, Etruscans, Hebrews, Arabs, Romans, and eventually almost everyone — the ancestor of nearly every alphabetic script in use today.

cahokia.context_blurb: Cahokia was the largest Native American city north of Mexico before Europeans arrived. It stood where modern St Louis is, on the floodplain of the Mississippi River, from about 600 to 1400 CE. At its peak around 1100 it had tens of thousands of inhabitants — larger than contemporary London — spread around a central plaza dominated by an enormous earthen pyramid called Monks Mound, still the biggest prehistoric earthwork in North America. The civilization that built it is called the Mississippian culture. Why it collapsed is still debated.

cairo-and-the-giza-pyramids.context_blurb: Cairo, on the Nile River in Egypt, is the largest city in the Arab world. Its medieval 'Islamic Cairo' is one of the oldest Islamic cities on Earth, founded in the 10th century and dense with mosques, minarets, markets, and madrasas. Just on the city's southwestern outskirts, within view of its newer suburbs, rise the three Giza pyramids — the only one of the ancient Seven Wonders of the World still standing — and the Great Sphinx. Few other cities on Earth telescope five thousand years of history into one skyline.

cape-town-and-table-mountain.context_blurb: Cape Town sits at the southwestern tip of Africa, where two oceans meet, under the sheer flat summit of Table Mountain. It was founded in the 17th century as a stopover for Dutch East India Company ships rounding the Cape of Good Hope, and it grew into one of the most spectacularly-sited cities in the world. The surrounding region hosts an entire floral kingdom of its own, with thousands of plant species found nowhere else on Earth. Just offshore lies the island where Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for most of his twenty-seven years in captivity.

cappadocia.context_blurb: Cappadocia is a region on the high central plateau of Turkey where volcanic ash has been eroded into a surreal landscape of pointed, often capped rock pinnacles that locals call 'fairy chimneys.' The soft rock made it very easy to carve, and for over a thousand years people here cut their houses, chapels, and whole multi-storey underground towns directly into the rock itself. Byzantine Christians took refuge from Arab raids in enormous underground cities beneath the surface. Today the region is famous for the dawn balloon-rides that drift above its chimneys.

cappadocia-and-the-derinkuyu-underground.context_blurb: The high plateau of Cappadocia in central Turkey is riddled with underground cities — multi-storey warrens of rooms, stables, wine-presses, churches, and air-shafts, cut level upon level into the soft volcanic rock. The largest known one is Derinkuyu, which could hide thousands of people for weeks at a time. They were used by Byzantine Christians during Arab raids in the Middle Ages. The most astonishing one was found in 1963 by a man renovating his basement.

caral.context_blurb: Caral, on the dry Pacific coast of Peru, is the oldest known city in the Americas, dating back to around 2600 BCE. That makes it a contemporary of the Egyptian pyramids. Its people lived in a desert valley, grew cotton, and traded with coastal fishing villages for anchovies. They built platform mounds, sunken circular plazas, and small flat-topped pyramids. Astonishingly, no sign of weapons, warfare, or defensive walls has been found at Caral; the earliest American civilization appears to have been a peaceful one.

carnac-the-breton-stone-alignments.context_blurb: On the Brittany coast of northwest France stand the Carnac stones: three thousand upright standing-stones ranged across the fields in orderly rows, some running for kilometres. They were raised by Neolithic farmers thousands of years before the pyramids, and nobody is quite sure why. Local folklore says they are an army of pagan soldiers turned to stone by a saint.

cartagena-de-indias.context_blurb: Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of modern Colombia, was for centuries the main Spanish port on mainland South America — the place where silver from the Andes was gathered for shipping back to Spain. Pirates, English privateers, and French admirals attacked it over and over, so the Spanish Crown wrapped the whole old town in some of the most elaborate stone fortifications ever built in the New World. Inside those walls the old city survives as a riot of pastel-coloured balconied houses, patios, and churches.

cenotes-sinkholes-to-a-flooded-underworl.context_blurb: A cenote is a natural sinkhole in the limestone bedrock, filled with crystal-clear groundwater. The Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico is probably the most cenote-rich region on Earth; thousands dot the surface, and most are connected underground into one of the longest cave-river systems in the world. The ancient Maya held cenotes sacred as entrances to the underworld, and some have given up jewellery, pottery, and human bones left there as offerings. Divers today map the submerged tunnels in multi-day expeditions.

chaco-canyon.context_blurb: Chaco Canyon, in modern northwestern New Mexico, was the political, religious, and ceremonial centre of a huge Ancestral Puebloan network between about 850 and 1150 CE. Its people built 'great houses' of several hundred rooms with multi-story walls of carefully fitted sandstone. Perfectly straight roads radiated out across the surrounding desert to distant outlier settlements. Some of the structures are aligned astronomically to catch the solstice sunlight. The civilization collapsed and left; its descendants are the Pueblo peoples of the modern Southwest.

chan-chan.context_blurb: Chan Chan, on the dry northern coast of Peru, was the capital of the Chimu civilization that preceded and briefly rivalled the Inca. It flourished from around 900 to 1470 CE. At its height Chan Chan held tens of thousands of people in nine great walled palace compounds, built entirely of mud brick, with walls decorated in geometric reliefs and sea-animal patterns. It is widely considered the largest city of pre-Columbian South America and the largest adobe city ever built on Earth.

chicago.context_blurb: Chicago grew up on the shore of Lake Michigan at a crucial portage between the Great Lakes watershed and the Mississippi watershed — a geographical hinge of the United States. In the 19th century it exploded into the country's great meatpacking and railroad hub, until in 1871 a huge fire burned much of it down. The rebuild made Chicago a laboratory for a new kind of city: the first true skyscrapers were engineered on its downtown 'Loop,' and some of American architecture's biggest names worked here.

chichen-itza.context_blurb: Chichen Itza, on the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico, was one of the greatest cities of the Maya world. It flourished from roughly 600 to 1200 CE and was a hybrid of classic Maya and Toltec architectural styles. Its central pyramid temple, El Castillo, is a precisely engineered stone calendar: on the spring and autumn equinoxes, the setting sun throws a shadow along one of its stairways that looks like a serpent slithering down the pyramid. Chichen Itza also has one of the largest and best-preserved Mesoamerican ball courts anywhere.

chocolate-hills-of-bohol.context_blurb: The Chocolate Hills on the island of Bohol in the central Philippines are a landscape of around a thousand nearly identical conical limestone hills, spread evenly across a flat plain for mile after mile. In the dry season, the grass that covers them turns brown — like chocolate — which is how they got their name. They were formed by millions of years of rainwater slowly dissolving the limestone, leaving the harder cores behind.

classic-karst-the-land-that-named-itself.context_blurb: The word 'karst' refers to any landscape where soluble rock, usually limestone, has been dissolved and eroded by water into a strange topography of caves, sinkholes, underground rivers, and jagged outcrops. The term comes from a specific plateau straddling the border of modern Slovenia and northeastern Italy, where this kind of landscape was first studied scientifically in the 19th century. The 'classic karst' of this region is still a textbook example — a dry stony plateau where surface rivers vanish into holes and reappear kilometres away.

cloud-forests-the-forests-in-the-clouds.context_blurb: Cloud forests are a rare kind of tropical mountain forest that spends most of its time wrapped in fog. They form at a particular altitude band — usually between about 1,500 and 3,000 metres — where moist air rising off warm lowlands cools and condenses into cloud, soaking everything in it. The trees are hung with mosses, orchids, bromeliads, and ferns growing not in soil but in each other. Cloud forests are extraordinarily biodiverse per hectare and are home to animals found nowhere else, like the resplendent quetzal and the olinguito.

coastal-forests-mangroves-and-kelp.context_blurb: The world's two most spectacular 'coastal forests' are not made of ordinary trees. In the tropics, dense tangles of mangroves — salt-tolerant trees with stilt-like roots — rise straight out of muddy saltwater coastlines, where they shelter fish nurseries and buffer the land against storms. In the cold waters off California, Chile, South Africa, and Tasmania, giant kelp grows upward through the sea in a swaying underwater forest where sea otters, seals, and leopard sharks move among the fronds. Both are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth.

cold-currents-and-the-coastal-deserts-th.context_blurb: Along the western coasts of several continents, cold ocean currents flow toward the equator from colder polar regions. These currents chill the air just above the sea, so that moisture condenses out before it can reach the land as rain. The result is that some of the driest deserts on Earth sit right against the ocean. The Atacama in Chile, the Namib in Namibia, and the coastal deserts of Baja California and the southwest Australian coast all exist because of this trick of the cold water offshore.

continental-drift-and-plate-tectonics.context_blurb: Plate tectonics is the big idea that explains almost all of Earth's geology on long timescales. The rigid outer shell of the planet is broken into a dozen or so great plates that drift slowly across the molten layer beneath them, carrying continents and ocean floors with them. Where plates pull apart, new ocean floor is born; where they crash together, mountains rise and earthquakes shake the land; where they slide past each other, faults grind. The theory took most of the 20th century to be accepted — the evidence of matching coastlines, fossils, and seafloor stripes finally made it undeniable.

continents-in-collision-the-great-mounta.context_blurb: Where two of Earth's continental tectonic plates slowly crash into each other, mountains rise. The ongoing collision between the Indian plate and the rest of Asia built the Himalayas and keeps pushing them up a few millimetres a year. Older but similar collisions built the Alps, the Zagros of Iran, the Urals, and more ancient ranges like the Appalachians. Looking at a modern mountain range is a way of reading, in slow motion, a collision that may have taken fifty million years to unfold.

coral-reefs-and-the-heat-that-bleaches-t.context_blurb: Coral reefs are built by tiny coral polyps, animals that live in colonies and secrete calcium carbonate skeletons. Over thousands of years those skeletons pile up into vast reef structures that are among the most biologically rich ecosystems on Earth. The coral animals themselves live in a tight partnership with microscopic algae that live inside their tissues and feed them. When the water gets too warm, corals eject the algae and lose their colour, in a process called 'bleaching'; if conditions don't return to normal fast enough, the corals starve to death.

crater-lake.context_blurb: Crater Lake, in the mountains of southern Oregon in the United States, sits in a nearly circular caldera that formed when the volcano Mount Mazama blew off its own top and collapsed about 7,700 years ago. Rainwater and snowmelt gradually filled the hollow, with no inlets or outlets, into one of the deepest and purest lakes in the country. Its water is so transparent that it absorbs blue light the way the open ocean does, giving the lake its unmistakable deep sapphire colour. The local Klamath people have a story about two gods battling in this landscape at the moment of the volcano's collapse.

cremona-the-town-of-stradivarius-violins.context_blurb: Cremona is a small city in northern Italy where, between roughly 1550 and 1750, several families of violin-makers invented and perfected the modern violin, viola, and cello. The best-known of these makers was Antonio Stradivari, who worked in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. Something about the wood, the varnish, the design, or the geometry of his instruments produced a sound that has never been convincingly surpassed, and surviving Stradivarius violins change hands today for millions of dollars. Precisely why they sound the way they do is still debated.

cuneiform-and-the-clay-tablets-of-sumer.context_blurb: Cuneiform is one of the earliest systems of writing ever developed. It was invented by the Sumerians in southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq) in the late 4th millennium BCE, when scribes began pressing wedge-shaped marks into wet clay tablets using a cut reed stylus. The clay was then dried in the sun or baked, which is one reason so many of the tablets have survived unchanged across more than 5,000 years. Over the centuries cuneiform was adapted for Akkadian, Babylonian, Hittite, and other languages across the Near East. It fell out of use around the end of the 1st century CE and was unreadable for the next 1,800 years.

cusco.context_blurb: Cusco, high in the Andes of modern Peru, was the capital of the Inca Empire — the Tawantinsuyu or 'four quarters joined' — when the Spanish arrived in 1533. The Inca designed their city as the sacred centre of their world; its layout traditionally mimics the outline of a crouching puma. The Spanish destroyed many Inca temples and built their own churches and palaces on top of the massive, impossibly tight-fitted Inca foundations, which is why most streets in the old town still have Inca stonework in their lower courses.

cusco-and-sacsayhuaman.context_blurb: Cusco, high in the Peruvian Andes, was the capital of the Inca Empire. Overlooking the city stands Sacsayhuaman, a huge stone-walled complex that may have served as both a fortress and a sacred ceremonial precinct. Its walls are built out of massive stone blocks fitted together with such precision that a sheet of paper cannot be slipped between them, without mortar. Some blocks weigh over 100 tonnes. How exactly the Inca shaped and set these stones is one of the enduring puzzles of pre-Columbian engineering.

cyrillic-and-the-brothers-of-thessalonik.context_blurb: The Cyrillic alphabet, used today for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian, and many other Slavic and Central Asian languages, grew out of the missionary work of two 9th-century Byzantine Greek brothers, Cyril and Methodius. They were sent from the city of Thessaloniki in northern Greece to Christianize the Slavic peoples of Central Europe, and to do so they invented a new alphabet suited to Slavic sounds. The one now called 'Cyrillic' is actually a later refinement; the pair's original invention is called Glagolitic.

dallol-and-the-danakil-depression.context_blurb: The Danakil Depression, in the Afar region of northern Ethiopia, is one of the lowest, hottest, and most alien places on Earth. It sits where three tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart. The hydrothermal field around Dallol bubbles with pools of sulphurous bright-yellow, green, and orange water, salt deserts, and lava-filled volcanic craters. Afar nomads still mine salt by hand here and transport it out on camel caravans, as they have for centuries.

damascus.context_blurb: Damascus, the capital of Syria, lies in an oasis at the eastern edge of the Mediterranean world. It has probably been continuously inhabited longer than any other city on Earth, with roots going back at least seven thousand years. In the 7th century it was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate, the first great Islamic empire. The city is still structured around its ancient Roman grid, with a straight main street mentioned by name in the New Testament. Its medieval quarter has been scarred by the fighting of the Syrian civil war.

damascus-steel-the-lost-watered-blades.context_blurb: 'Damascus steel' is a famous type of sword blade that was forged somewhere in the Islamic world between about the 9th and 17th centuries, from a kind of raw ingot imported from southern India and Sri Lanka. The finished blades had a mesmerizing swirling pattern in the metal — like watered silk — and were fabulously sharp and strong. Then, in the 18th century, the technique vanished. For centuries no modern smith could reproduce it. Only in recent decades has materials science begun to understand what the medieval smiths were doing.

death-valley.context_blurb: Death Valley, in eastern California, is the lowest, driest, and hottest place in North America. The valley floor sits below sea level and is enclosed by high mountain ranges that squeeze almost all the moisture out of the air before it can reach the valley. In summer, air temperatures regularly climb above 50 degrees Celsius. The valley got its name from a group of pioneers who got stuck trying to cross it in 1849; most survived.

delhi-the-city-of-seven-cities.context_blurb: Delhi, in northern India, is often called the 'city of seven cities' because successive rulers kept founding new capitals on nearby sites rather than reusing the old ones. Its layered ruins span more than a thousand years — Hindu, Muslim, Mughal, and British. Among the many monuments scattered through modern Delhi are a mysterious ancient iron pillar that stubbornly refuses to rust, a towering medieval victory minaret of carved red sandstone, and a vast walled fort from which Mughal emperors ruled much of the subcontinent.

delphi-the-oracle-at-the-navel-of-the-wo.context_blurb: Delphi, perched on the steep slopes of Mount Parnassus in central Greece, held the most important oracle of the ancient Mediterranean world. For roughly a thousand years, Greeks and foreigners climbed up to its sanctuary of Apollo to put questions to a priestess whose cryptic answers decided wars, colonies, and marriages. The ancient Greeks considered the spot to be the exact centre of the Earth. Over the sanctuary gate were carved two short Greek maxims that have echoed through Western philosophy ever since.

denali.context_blurb: Denali, in central Alaska, is the highest peak in North America at over 6,100 metres. Although it is not quite as tall as some Asian or South American giants, it has one of the greatest vertical reliefs of any mountain on Earth, rising almost entirely from near-sea-level lowland rather than from an already-high plateau. Its name in the Koyukon Athabascan language means roughly 'the tall one.' For a century it was officially called Mount McKinley; the United States restored its native name in 2015.

devils-tower.context_blurb: Devil's Tower, in northeastern Wyoming in the United States, is an isolated stump of igneous rock rising about 265 metres straight up out of a prairie of sagebrush and ponderosa pine. It was formed when a plume of molten rock pushed up into surrounding sedimentary rock and cooled; the softer rocks around it later eroded away, leaving this hard core standing. Several Native American peoples hold the tower sacred and have their own stories about its origin. In 1906 it was named the very first National Monument in the United States.

drainage-basins-and-the-continental-divi.context_blurb: A drainage basin is the area of land from which all surface water eventually flows into the same river mouth or lake. Big continents are divided by 'continental divides' — ridgelines separating basins that drain to different oceans. In North America, water on the eastern side of the Rockies ends up in the Atlantic or the Gulf of Mexico; water on the western side ends up in the Pacific. There is also a 'triple divide' point in Montana where a single raindrop could in principle be fated for the Atlantic, Pacific, or Arctic Ocean.

drumlins-and-eskers-streamlined-hills-an.context_blurb: A drumlin is a smooth, elongated hill of sediment left behind by a passing ice sheet; eskers are long winding ridges of sand and gravel that mark the beds of ancient rivers that once ran through tunnels under the ice. Both are telltale fossils of the great ice-age glaciers that once covered large parts of North America and Europe. Entire 'drumlin fields' of hundreds of look-alike hills decorate parts of Ireland, Wisconsin, and upstate New York. Looking at them is like reading the fine print on an invisible map of where the ice flowed.

dubai.context_blurb: Dubai is a city-state on the Persian Gulf coast of the United Arab Emirates. Within living memory it was a small desert port whose economy ran on pearling and the dhow trade with India and East Africa. From the 1970s on, oil money and then explicit government policy transformed it into one of the most relentlessly built-up cities on Earth, with the world's tallest skyscraper rising from the desert, artificial palm-shaped islands reclaimed from the sea, and indoor ski slopes beside the mall.

dubrovnik.context_blurb: Dubrovnik is a small Croatian city on the Adriatic coast, protected by a complete, walkable ring of medieval stone city walls. For centuries it existed as a tiny maritime trading republic — the Republic of Ragusa — that cleverly outmaneuvered the Venetians, the Ottomans, and the Habsburgs to stay independent. Its merchants rivalled Venice's. The old city, famously filmed as 'King's Landing' in the Game of Thrones TV series, is a tight warren of smooth-paved marble streets and terracotta roofs inside the walls.

easter-island-rapa-nui.context_blurb: Easter Island — called Rapa Nui by its own people — is one of the most isolated inhabited islands on Earth, in the far southeastern Pacific. Polynesian settlers arrived there sometime between about 900 and 1200 CE. Over the following centuries they carved and raised nearly a thousand enormous stone statues of ancestral figures, called moai. The population later collapsed, through some combination of ecological strain, European contact, slave raids, and introduced diseases. The island is a Chilean possession today, and its people are still here.

egyptian-hieroglyphs-and-the-rosetta-sto.context_blurb: Egyptian hieroglyphs are the picture-based writing system used for sacred and monumental texts throughout the three thousand years of pharaonic civilization. After the Roman era, no one could read them anymore, and for about 1,400 years the elaborate carvings in Egyptian temples were a complete mystery. The key to cracking them turned out to be a slab of stone that soldiers in Napoleon's 1799 Egyptian campaign stumbled on near a village in the Nile Delta: it bore the same royal decree carved in three scripts, one of which was readable Greek. A French scholar, Jean-Francois Champollion, eventually used it to unlock the hieroglyphs in the 1820s.

el-nino-and-la-nina-the-pacific-that-shi.context_blurb: El Nino and La Nina are the two phases of a natural climate cycle in the tropical Pacific Ocean. Normally the trade winds push warm surface water westward, piling it up near Indonesia and letting cold deep water rise near South America. In an El Nino year that pattern breaks down and the warm water sloshes east; in a La Nina year it is reinforced. The resulting shifts in sea temperatures ripple through the atmosphere and change weather patterns across much of the world — floods in some places, droughts in others, fewer or more hurricanes.

ellora-kailasa-temple.context_blurb: At the Ellora caves in western India stands what may be the most audacious single sculpture ever made. The Kailasa Temple, honouring the Hindu god Shiva, is not a built temple at all; it was carved downward out of a single cliff of solid basalt in the 8th century CE, with full courtyards, towers, elephants, and pillars all left standing as the surrounding rock was cut away. The volume of stone removed to free it is staggering.

endorheic-basins-water-with-no-way-out-t.context_blurb: An endorheic basin is a drainage basin from which no water ever reaches the ocean. Rain and snowmelt flow in but can only escape by evaporation. Over long time scales this concentrates whatever salts and minerals the inflow carried, so endorheic basins often hold salty lakes, salt flats, or expanses of mineral-crusted desert. The Caspian Sea, Great Salt Lake, Lake Chad, the Aral Sea, and the Bolivian Salar de Uyuni are all endorheic. About 18 percent of the Earth's land surface drains to no sea at all.

estuaries-and-tidal-bores-where-river-me.context_blurb: An estuary is the stretch of a river where fresh water meets and mixes with the salt water of the sea, usually at the river's mouth. Estuaries are among the most biologically productive habitats on Earth, nurseries for fish and shellfish. Many of them show interesting hydrology: as the tide pushes salty water upstream, the fresh river water sits above it in a wedge-shaped layer. In narrow, funnel-shaped estuaries, the rising tide can even combine into a travelling wave that races upriver, called a tidal bore.

etna-stromboli-and-the-word-volcano.context_blurb: Along the coast of Italy and Sicily sit several of the most famous active volcanoes on Earth. Mount Etna on Sicily is Europe's tallest active volcano and one of the most active anywhere; it has been erupting on and off for thousands of years. Just offshore to the north, the small volcanic island of Stromboli has been in a state of near-continuous mild eruption for several thousand years. The English word 'volcano' itself comes from another island of this chain, Vulcano, which the Romans believed to be the forge of their god of fire.

fado-lisbon.context_blurb: Fado is the melancholic urban folk music of Portugal, born in the port-side neighborhoods of Lisbon in the first half of the 19th century. Its name comes from the Latin fatum ('fate'). It is typically sung by a solo singer accompanied by a classical guitar and a distinctively pear-shaped Portuguese guitar, and its lyrics are preoccupied with a particular Portuguese emotion of bittersweet longing for things lost or far away. In 2011 UNESCO added fado to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

fatehpur-sikri-the-abandoned-red-city.context_blurb: Fatehpur Sikri, in northern India near Agra, is a perfectly preserved red-sandstone imperial city built in the late 16th century by the Mughal emperor Akbar as his new capital. Akbar held religious debates in it between Muslims, Hindus, Christians, Jains, and Zoroastrians, trying to arrive at a sort of universal faith. Then, after only a handful of years, the city was abandoned, apparently because its water supply failed. It stands today in near-mint condition as a frozen snapshot of the Mughal court at its most ambitious.

fes.context_blurb: Fes (Fez), in Morocco, was founded in the 8th century CE and became for a time the capital of a succession of medieval Muslim dynasties in North Africa. Its old walled medina — a maze of lanes too narrow for cars — is one of the largest living medieval urban environments anywhere, little changed in a thousand years. Donkeys still carry loads through its alleys. Fes is home to what is often described as the oldest continuously operating university in the world, founded in 859 by a Tunisian woman named Fatima al-Fihri.

fjords-drowned-glacier-valleys.context_blurb: A fjord is a deep, narrow sea-inlet with high, often sheer, rock walls. Fjords form where glaciers running down to the sea gouged out deep U-shaped valleys during an ice age; when the ice melted and sea levels rose, the sea flooded in and drowned the valleys. Norway's long western coast is famous for its fjords; others carve the coasts of Chile, New Zealand, Alaska, Greenland, and the Canadian Arctic. The water in them can be deeper than the open ocean just outside the fjord's mouth.

flamenco-andalusia.context_blurb: Flamenco is the dance and music tradition born in Andalusia, the southernmost region of Spain, out of a centuries-long cultural mix: Andalusian, Roma, Jewish, and Moorish. It combines passionate guitar playing, hand-clapping, foot-stamping, singing, and dance in a highly structured but intensely emotional performance. Different flamenco 'palos' (styles) carry very different moods, from grief-stricken siguiriya to joyful alegrias. UNESCO recognized flamenco in 2010 as part of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

florence-brunelleschis-impossible-dome.context_blurb: Florence, in Tuscany, Italy, was the city where the Renaissance began. Under the enormous wealth and patronage of the Medici family of bankers, it produced a staggering roster of 15th- and 16th-century painters, sculptors, and architects — Donatello, Botticelli, Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci. Its cathedral is crowned by a vast red-brick dome designed by the goldsmith-turned-architect Filippo Brunelleschi, who had to invent entirely new techniques to build the biggest dome anyone had attempted since Roman times.

foehn-and-chinook-the-warm-wind-off-the-.context_blurb: When moist air is forced up and over a mountain range, it drops its rain on the windward side; by the time it reaches the leeward slope it is dry. As it then sinks down the far side, the air is compressed and warms rapidly, sometimes dramatically — temperatures can rise by 20 degrees Celsius in minutes. In the Alps this warm dry downslope wind is called the Foehn; in the Rockies the Chinook; in southern California the Santa Ana; in Argentina the Zonda. The phenomenon has been linked to headaches, forest fires, and avalanches.

from-rift-to-ocean-the-red-sea-and-the-a.context_blurb: Where two continental tectonic plates pull apart, a long linear valley slowly opens between them, called a rift. If the rift keeps spreading long enough, the sea eventually floods in and a new ocean basin is born. The Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden are examples of rifts that have reached the ocean stage; the East African Rift to their south is a continental rift that is still in its earlier stages. At the Afar Triangle in Ethiopia, three plates meet and are tearing one of the strangest low-lying hot landscapes on the planet.

g-bekli-tepe.context_blurb: On a hilltop in southeastern Turkey stands a cluster of carved stone pillars arranged in rings, decorated with reliefs of foxes, snakes, scorpions, and birds. What makes them extraordinary is their age: about 11,500 years old, which means they were raised by Stone Age people before the invention of pottery, metal, or farming. Gobekli Tepe has rewritten the textbook timeline of civilization, suggesting that organized ritual and monumental building came before agriculture, not after. Equally strange, the whole site was deliberately buried under rubble around 8000 BCE and forgotten for ten thousand years.

ggantija-and-maltas-megalithic-temples.context_blurb: The tiny Mediterranean island nation of Malta hides a staggering secret: its stone temples are older than the Egyptian pyramids. Built by a mysterious prehistoric people roughly 5,500 years ago, the Ggantija temples on Gozo are among the oldest free-standing structures ever raised anywhere. Local legend said they were built by a race of giants, which is where the name comes from. The civilisation that built them later vanished without obvious explanation.

giant-waves-and-where-the-sea-floor-buil.context_blurb: Some stretches of coastline consistently produce the biggest ocean waves on Earth. Nazare on the Portuguese coast is one; Teahupo'o in Tahiti is another; Mavericks on the California coast is a third. The reason is almost always the shape of the sea floor just offshore. Deep underwater canyons focus incoming swells and funnel their energy toward the surface, so that waves which look ordinary further out suddenly rear up into towering walls just before they hit the beach. These spots have become legendary in big-wave surfing.

giants-causeway-and-fingals-cave.context_blurb: Along the north coast of Northern Ireland, a stretch of the shore is paved with roughly 40,000 interlocking black stone columns, mostly hexagonal, stepping out into the sea. On the opposite side of the water, on the Scottish island of Staffa, Fingal's Cave is a natural cathedral formed from the same honeycomb columns. Both were formed about 60 million years ago when enormous sheets of lava cooled and cracked in orderly polygonal patterns. The local Irish legend attributes them to a battle between two giants, one Irish and one Scottish.

glacial-erratics-boulders-the-ice-carrie.context_blurb: A glacial erratic is a large boulder sitting at the surface of the land whose rock type does not match the bedrock around it, because an ice-age glacier picked it up somewhere far away and dropped it off when the ice melted. Some erratics are the size of houses. In 19th-century Europe, before glaciation was understood, erratics were often explained as having been left by the biblical Flood; the Swiss geologist Louis Agassiz was one of the first to argue they had been moved by ice.

gondar.context_blurb: Gondar, in the mountains of northern Ethiopia, was the imperial capital of the Christian kingdom of Ethiopia from the 17th into the 19th century. Its emperors built a cluster of stone castles there — real European-style castles with crenellated walls and towers — which looks surprising enough that visitors sometimes rub their eyes. Ethiopia was never colonized, so the royal line goes back in an unbroken thread to its ancient roots; the Gondar castles are evidence of a confident, outward-looking court that borrowed what it fancied from the wider world.

gor-e-island.context_blurb: Goree is a small island just off the coast of Dakar, in modern Senegal, that was fought over and traded between the Portuguese, Dutch, English, and French for several centuries. It is remembered today chiefly as a site of the Atlantic slave trade. Its 'House of Slaves,' with its narrow passages and a doorway opening onto the water, has become a place of pilgrimage, visited by both Nelson Mandela and Barack Obama; serious historians argue over how many Africans actually passed through this specific island, but it remains a powerful symbol of a brutal chapter in history.

granada-the-alhambras-water-palace.context_blurb: Granada, in southern Spain, was the last Muslim-ruled kingdom in Western Europe. For centuries after the rest of the Iberian Peninsula had been reconquered by Christian kings, Granada held out as the capital of the small Nasrid emirate; it finally fell in 1492 to Ferdinand and Isabella. On a hill above the city stands the Alhambra palace-fortress, a masterpiece of Islamic architecture: a complex of courtyards, fountains, and halls whose walls are covered in intricate stucco calligraphy and geometric patterns.

great-zimbabwe.context_blurb: Great Zimbabwe is the ruin of a medieval African city in the south of today's country of Zimbabwe, which is actually named after it. From roughly the 11th to the 15th centuries it was the thriving capital of a wealthy Shona kingdom that controlled the inland trade in gold and ivory, selling it on toward the Indian Ocean coast. Its most famous surviving feature is the Great Enclosure, a towering circuit of stone walls built entirely without mortar, with a mysterious conical tower rising inside. For centuries European visitors refused to believe Africans could have built it; modern archaeology has settled that argument.

groundwater-the-hidden-rivers-under-our-.context_blurb: Groundwater is water held underground in the tiny spaces inside porous rock and soil, in layers called aquifers. It is replenished by rainwater soaking down from the surface over long periods — sometimes thousands of years. Across much of the world, from the US Great Plains to north Africa to north China, agriculture and cities depend heavily on pumping groundwater. In some places this pumping is now extracting water much faster than nature puts it back, with consequences from sinking land to drying wells.

gyeongju-the-museum-without-walls.context_blurb: Gyeongju, in southeastern South Korea, was for a thousand years the capital of the Silla kingdom, which eventually unified the Korean peninsula around the 7th century. The whole city is studded with grassy royal burial mounds that look like small natural hills but are actually gigantic tombs full of golden crowns, jewelry, and horse-fittings. Pagodas, Buddhist carvings, and old temples are everywhere. Gyeongju is sometimes called 'the museum without walls' because so much of its ancient fabric is scattered across the modern town.

ha-long-bay.context_blurb: Ha Long Bay, on the northern coast of Vietnam, is a scatter of hundreds of steep-sided limestone pinnacles and islets rising out of the sea. The towers are what geologists call 'drowned tower karst': they were once hills in a limestone landscape on dry land, until the sea rose at the end of the last Ice Age and flooded the valleys between them. According to Vietnamese tradition, the islands were made when a dragon spat jewels into the sea.

hangul-the-alphabet-korea-designed-on-pu.context_blurb: Hangul is the alphabet used today for the Korean language. Unlike most writing systems, which evolved slowly over centuries, Hangul was deliberately designed from scratch by a single person: King Sejong the Great, who announced it in 1446. He explicitly wanted a system simple enough that any Korean farmer could learn to read and write, instead of relying on the thousands of Chinese characters that only an elite could master. Hangul's letters are famously systematic — each one is shaped to resemble the position of the mouth, tongue, and throat when making that sound.

hanoi-old-quarter.context_blurb: Hanoi, the capital of Vietnam, grew up on the banks of the Red River in the north of the country. For the last thousand years it has been one of the great cities of Vietnam, which spent much of its history fending off China from the north and (in modern times) France and the United States from across the oceans. The 'Old Quarter' is a dense 36-street warren of narrow 'tube houses,' each lane traditionally dedicated to selling a single kind of good — silver, silk, bamboo, tin — a layout that still shapes the neighbourhood today.

harar.context_blurb: Harar is a walled Muslim city in eastern Ethiopia that for centuries guarded a crossroads of the trans-African caravan trade. Its old quarter is a tight medieval warren of lanes behind thick stone walls, with dozens of small mosques inside, and it is traditionally counted as one of the great holy cities of the Muslim world. The French poet Arthur Rimbaud lived here for years as a trader after giving up poetry. Harar is also famous for a peculiar nightly ritual that takes place just outside its walls after dark.

harris-tweed-the-cloth-protected-by-law.context_blurb: Harris Tweed is a kind of thick woollen cloth woven on the Outer Hebrides islands of northwestern Scotland. The weavers live and work in the Isle of Harris, Lewis, Uist, and Barra. Harris Tweed is so distinctive that in 1909 the British Parliament passed a law reserving its name for cloth woven at the weavers' own homes from pure virgin wool, dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides, and stamped by the industry's own authentication board. It is the only textile in the world protected by an Act of Parliament.

havana.context_blurb: Havana is the capital of Cuba, founded by the Spanish in 1519 on an excellent natural harbour on the island's north coast. For centuries it was the fortified gathering-point of Spain's silver-fleet convoys back to Europe. In 1959 Fidel Castro's revolution took power, Cuba became a Soviet ally, and the United States imposed a long embargo. Havana's old quarter, suspended somewhere between gorgeously faded Spanish-colonial grandeur and 1950s Chevrolets, is now one of the most atmospheric city centres in the Americas.

hip-hop-the-bronx.context_blurb: Hip-hop was born in the 1970s in the Bronx, one of the five boroughs of New York City. In its early years it coalesced out of block parties, basement discotheques, and DJ battles in the then-poor Bronx neighborhoods. From that scene emerged four fundamental elements — DJing, MCing (rapping), breakdancing, and graffiti art — that together make up hip-hop culture. Within fifty years it had become probably the single most influential cultural movement of the late 20th and early 21st centuries, dominating global popular music.

hiroshima-the-city-that-came-back.context_blurb: Hiroshima is a Japanese city on the southwestern coast of Honshu. On August 6, 1945, the United States dropped the first atomic bomb ever used in war on it, killing tens of thousands outright and tens of thousands more from radiation sickness and injury. In the decades since, the city has rebuilt itself and become a global symbol of peace. At the hypocentre, a single ruined domed building has been left standing in its blasted state as a memorial, while the surrounding streets throng with ordinary modern life.

hoi-an.context_blurb: Hoi An is a small town on the central coast of Vietnam. Between about the 15th and 19th centuries it was one of the busiest trading ports in Southeast Asia, with Japanese, Chinese, Dutch, Portuguese, and French merchants all based there. When the river harbour silted up, trade moved elsewhere and Hoi An slept. Its old quarter — a mix of wooden Chinese shophouses, a Japanese covered bridge, and French-colonial additions — survived almost intact. Today it is beautifully lit at night by thousands of coloured silk lanterns strung across its lanes.

holy-confluences-and-the-lowest-river-on.context_blurb: Many religions treat the place where two rivers join — a confluence — as particularly sacred, because the mixing of waters is an obvious symbol of unity. The most famous example is the Sangam at Prayagraj in northern India, where the Ganges meets the Yamuna and a tradition says they are joined underneath by a third, invisible, mythical river. Every twelve years tens of millions of Hindu pilgrims gather there for the Kumbh Mela. Elsewhere in sacred geography, the Jordan River flows down to the lowest point on Earth.

hong-kong-the-vertical-city.context_blurb: Hong Kong is a cluster of islands and a bit of mainland in the Pearl River Delta of southern China. For 150 years it was a British colony, which is why its civic life is a strange blend of Chinese and English habits. Returned to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, it has one of the most dramatic urban landscapes on Earth: steep green hills tumbling straight into a sheltered harbour, with its downtown pinned between them in a wall of improbably slender skyscrapers. It has long been one of Asia's great financial centres and probably the city with the most skyscrapers in the world.

hotspots-the-island-chains-a-drifting-pl.context_blurb: A 'hotspot' is a plume of unusually hot material rising from deep inside the Earth that stays roughly fixed while the tectonic plate above it drifts past. The hotspot melts the overlying plate again and again, building a chain of volcanoes. The Hawaiian island chain is the textbook example: the active volcano is at one end of the chain, and the islands get older and more weathered the further you move along it, charting the direction the Pacific plate has been moving over tens of millions of years. Yellowstone is another, less obvious, example.

hue-imperial-citadel.context_blurb: Hue, on the Perfume River in central Vietnam, was the imperial capital of Vietnam under the Nguyen dynasty from 1802 to 1945. In its centre is a huge moated and walled imperial citadel, modelled consciously on Beijing's Forbidden City. Much of it was heavily damaged during the Battle of Hue in 1968, one of the longest and bloodiest engagements of the Vietnam War, and some of it has only recently been restored.

hurricane-typhoon-cyclone-one-storm-thre.context_blurb: A hurricane, a typhoon, and a cyclone are the same kind of storm — a rotating tropical system of thunderstorms organized around a low-pressure centre — called by different names in different parts of the world. 'Hurricane' is used in the Atlantic and the northeastern Pacific, 'typhoon' in the northwestern Pacific, and simply 'cyclone' in the South Pacific and Indian Oceans. All of them form over warm tropical seas and feed on the energy of warm sea-surface water. Their most dangerous feature is often not the wind itself but the storm surge they push ahead of them.

ice-age-megafloods-and-vanished-lakes.context_blurb: At the end of the last Ice Age, as the great North American ice sheet melted, water piled up behind glacier-ice dams in enormous lakes. From time to time those dams broke. The results were megafloods — catastrophic torrents that lasted days or weeks, released more water than the combined flow of all the modern rivers on Earth, and ripped huge channels across the landscape. One such flood system, in what is now eastern Washington state, carved out the strange, scoured Channeled Scablands.

icebergs-how-they-calve-and-drift.context_blurb: Icebergs are chunks of freshwater ice that have broken off ('calved') from the edges of glaciers or ice shelves and drifted out into the sea. Most of the mass of an iceberg sits underwater, with only a small part showing above the surface. In the Southern Hemisphere, Antarctic ice shelves calve giant tabular icebergs; the biggest ever recorded was larger than the island of Jamaica. In the Northern Hemisphere, icebergs mostly come from the glaciers of Greenland and drift south in the Labrador Current, which is where the Titanic struck one in 1912.

iceland-where-two-continents-pull-apart.context_blurb: Iceland sits in the middle of the North Atlantic, straddling the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart. The island is literally splitting in half, a few centimetres per year. New land is also forming all the time: Iceland is one of the most volcanically active places on Earth, with eruptions somewhere on the island on average every few years. The combination of hot volcanic rock close to the surface and abundant rain-and-snowmelt makes Iceland the world's leader in geothermal energy.

iguaz-falls.context_blurb: Iguazu Falls crashes down a long curved cliff on the border of Argentina and Brazil, in the subtropical rainforests of South America. Rather than one broad sheet, the river splits over the edge into a long chain of individual cascades divided by lush rocky islands, so visitors can walk among the different drops. Depending on the water level the number of cascades varies, but it is always far more than Niagara. When the American First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt first saw the falls, she is said to have murmured, 'Poor Niagara!'

isfahan.context_blurb: Isfahan, in central Iran, was the capital of the Safavid Persian Empire in the 16th and 17th centuries under Shah Abbas the Great. A medieval Persian saying held that 'Isfahan is half the world,' and the shah built himself a city to match: an enormous central square ringed by palaces, a grand mosque, and a dazzling royal mosque, all faced in blue tilework. The Safavid Isfahan has survived largely intact; it is one of the most beautiful cities in the Islamic world.

isostatic-rebound-the-land-still-rising.context_blurb: The weight of a thick ice sheet pushes down on the Earth's crust, slowly bowing it into the softer mantle beneath. When the ice melts away, the crust springs back up — not all at once, but over thousands of years. This process is called isostatic rebound. It is still happening today in regions that were under the ice during the last Ice Age — Scandinavia, Scotland, and much of Canada are all literally rising upward every year, and the land along the Baltic coast of Sweden and Finland keeps gaining new metres of beachfront each generation.

istanbul.context_blurb: Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus strait in modern Turkey, with half the city in Europe and the other half in Asia. For most of its history it was Constantinople, capital first of the Christian Byzantine Empire from 330 CE and then, after the Ottoman conquest of 1453, capital of the Muslim Ottoman Empire for another 470 years. The city is layered: the great Byzantine cathedral of Hagia Sophia stands beside grand Ottoman mosques, built in deliberate imitation. The old walls that defended it for a thousand years still ring the historic peninsula.

jaipur-the-pink-city-and-its-stone-sky-m.context_blurb: Jaipur, in the desert state of Rajasthan in northwestern India, was founded in 1727 by Maharaja Jai Singh II. He was a serious astronomer as well as a king, and he laid out his new city on a geometric plan straight from classical Hindu town-planning texts. The old city was later painted a uniform warm pinkish red to welcome a visiting royal, and the colour has stuck. Jai Singh also built a bizarre open-air observatory of gigantic masonry sundials and quadrants there, built big because he mistrusted the little brass European instruments of his day.

jazz-new-orleans.context_blurb: Jazz was born in New Orleans at the turn of the 20th century, out of the extraordinary cultural blend of that city: African, Caribbean, French, Spanish, and Anglo-American traditions all layered on top of each other. Marching band music, blues, ragtime, church spirituals, and Creole songs all fed into it, and the result was a brand-new improvisational music built on syncopated rhythms, blue notes, and solo improvisation. From New Orleans it travelled up the Mississippi to Chicago and then east to New York, and from there to the world.

jerusalems-old-city-quarter-by-quarter.context_blurb: The old walled city of Jerusalem is the single most densely sacred square kilometre in the world. It is holy to the three Abrahamic faiths: for Jews, as the city of David and the site of the destroyed First and Second Temples; for Christians, as the city where Jesus was crucified and (they believe) rose from the dead; for Muslims, as the city from which Muhammad is held to have ascended on his Night Journey. The old city is traditionally divided into four quarters — Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian — tightly packed inside a 16th-century Ottoman wall.

jingdezhen-chinas-porcelain-capital.context_blurb: Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi province in southeastern China, has been China's porcelain-making capital for more than a thousand years. Imperial porcelain for the Chinese court was fired here from the 14th century onward. The clay around the town, mixed in the right proportions and fired at the right temperature, produces the thin, white, translucent ceramic that the English language simply calls 'china' after the country where it was invented. For centuries Europeans tried and failed to work out how to make it.

k2.context_blurb: K2 straddles the border of Pakistan and China in the Karakoram range. At 8,611 metres it is the second-highest mountain on Earth, only about 240 metres shorter than Everest, but it is a far more technical and dangerous climb. Roughly one in four climbers who has reached its summit has died either coming down or trying. K2 gets its utilitarian name from an old 19th-century British survey list; the mountain is in such a remote region that it has no widely-used local name.

kabuki-and-noh-japan.context_blurb: Noh and Kabuki are the two great traditional Japanese theatrical forms. Noh is the older of the two, dating to the 14th century: a slow, austere, highly stylized form of masked theatre favoured by the samurai elite. Kabuki arose in the early 1600s, more boisterous, colourful, and crowd-pleasing, drawing audiences from the merchant classes of the big cities. Both are still performed today, with roles passed from one generation of actors to the next within specific family lineages.

kano.context_blurb: Kano, in northern Nigeria, is one of the oldest cities of West Africa and for a thousand years has been a major terminus of the trans-Saharan caravan trade in salt, cloth, and leather. It is the heart of the Hausa people's homeland, now a city of several million, encircled by surviving stretches of a vast medieval earthen wall. Its dyeing pits, where cloth is turned deep indigo blue, have been in continuous use for about five hundred years.

karnak-and-ancient-thebes-luxor.context_blurb: Karnak, on the east bank of the Nile at modern Luxor, is the biggest religious complex ever built in the ancient world. Successive pharaohs across more than a thousand years each added their own temples, obelisks, chapels, and pylons to the site, piling up a sacred city of stone around a shared great temple to the god Amun-Ra. Its hall of columns is so dense and gigantic that walking into it feels like entering a petrified forest.

kente-the-ashanti-cloth-of-ghana.context_blurb: Kente is the brilliantly coloured strip-woven cloth of the Ashanti and Ewe peoples of Ghana and Togo in West Africa. Each piece is built up from narrow strips of handwoven fabric, about four inches wide, hand-sewn together edge to edge. Every pattern and colour combination carries a specific name and meaning, and traditional kente was once reserved for royalty. In modern times it has become a global symbol of African identity, worn at graduations and ceremonies far beyond West Africa.

kettle-lakes-where-buried-ice-melted.context_blurb: A kettle lake forms when a chunk of ice from a retreating glacier gets buried in sediment and then slowly melts under the ground. The ground above collapses and the resulting hollow fills with water. The thousands of small round lakes dotting places like Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Ontario, and parts of Scandinavia are mostly kettle lakes. From the air, a landscape pocked with them looks almost like it was dimpled with a thumb.

khiva-the-walled-desert-city.context_blurb: Khiva is a tiny, almost perfectly preserved medieval walled city in the middle of a Central Asian desert, in modern Uzbekistan. It was once a notorious Silk Road slave market and the capital of the Khanate of Khiva. Its old quarter — the Itchan Kala — is enclosed by thick mud-brick ramparts and crammed with blue-tiled madrasas, minarets, and mausoleums packed into a small walkable rectangle, which looks like a stage set when the sun lights it up at dawn.

kilimanjaro.context_blurb: Kilimanjaro, in northern Tanzania near the Kenyan border, is the highest mountain in Africa and the tallest free-standing mountain in the world — a huge volcanic cone rising out of the East African savannah. It is capped by glaciers even though it sits only three degrees south of the equator, though those ice fields have been shrinking fast over the last century. Unlike most of the world's great peaks, Kilimanjaro can be hiked rather than technically climbed, which is why thousands of trekkers summit it each year.

kilwa-kisiwani.context_blurb: Kilwa Kisiwani is a tiny island just off the coast of today's Tanzania that was once the richest trading city of the East African 'Swahili Coast.' Between about 1100 and 1500 its merchants were middlemen between the gold mines of inland Africa and the great trade routes of the Indian Ocean, dealing with ships from Arabia, Persia, India, and China. The 14th-century Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta called it one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Its stone palaces, mosques, and harbour buildings now stand in ruin, but they are among the oldest surviving stone buildings in sub-Saharan Africa.

kintsugi-japans-golden-mending.context_blurb: Kintsugi is the traditional Japanese art of repairing broken pottery by filling the cracks with a lacquer mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum. The resulting mended object is not disguised to look unbroken; instead the repair is highlighted, so the piece's history of breakage becomes a visible, often beautiful, part of the finished object. The practice is tied to a Japanese aesthetic philosophy — wabi-sabi — that finds beauty in imperfection, age, and incompleteness.

knossos-the-minoan-palace-and-the-labyri.context_blurb: On the Greek island of Crete stand the ruins of the Bronze Age palace of Knossos, centre of the Minoan civilisation that flourished around 2000 to 1400 BCE. Its sprawling, many-roomed plan may be the real-world origin of the Greek legend of the Minotaur hidden in a maze. The palace's wall-paintings show elegant women, fantastical animals, and a dangerous athletic ritual involving charging bulls. In the early 1900s the archaeologist Sir Arthur Evans dug it up and controversially rebuilt large parts of it with modern materials — his restorations are what tourists see today.

konark-sun-temple.context_blurb: On the eastern coast of India in the state of Odisha stands the 13th-century Konark temple, dedicated to the Hindu sun-god Surya. The whole structure was designed to look like a cosmic vehicle: an immense stone building shaped as a chariot, complete with carved wheels, prancing horses, and intricate reliefs on every surface. European sailors used it as a landmark. Most of its tallest tower collapsed centuries ago, but what remains is one of the great sculptural achievements of medieval India.

krakatoa-1883-the-loudest-sound-on-earth.context_blurb: In August 1883, the small volcanic island of Krakatoa, in the Sunda Strait between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra, exploded in one of the largest volcanic eruptions in recorded history. The main blast was heard thousands of kilometres away. The eruption triggered towering tsunamis that killed tens of thousands of people on surrounding coasts. Enough ash and sulphur was thrown into the stratosphere that global temperatures dropped by about a degree over the following years and sunsets everywhere turned strange colours.

krakow.context_blurb: Krakow is one of the oldest cities in Poland and was its royal capital from the 11th century until the court moved to Warsaw in 1596. The old town, built around a huge central market square, survived World War II nearly intact — unlike Warsaw, which was almost totally destroyed. Krakow is also the city where John Paul II was archbishop before being elected pope, and it sits very close to the German concentration camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau, a mere hour's drive away.

kyoto-the-thousand-year-capital-of-templ.context_blurb: Kyoto was the imperial capital of Japan for more than a thousand years, from 794 CE until the court moved to Tokyo in 1869.
