During the Second World War the United States specifically spared the city from heavy bombing because of its cultural importance, which means its wooden temples, stone-and-gravel gardens, Shinto shrines, and traditional geisha quarters survive essentially intact. It is home to seventeen UNESCO World Heritage sites. The classical arts of Japan — tea ceremony, ikebana, Noh drama, kaiseki cuisine — all took their mature form here.

la-paz-and-el-alto.context_blurb: La Paz, in Bolivia, is the highest capital city on Earth — not quite the official constitutional capital, but the de facto seat of government. It sits in a deep canyon in the Andes at around 3,600 metres above sea level. On the plateau above the canyon's rim sprawls El Alto, a vast younger city of indigenous Aymara migrants that has become one of the largest cities of Bolivia in its own right. Modern cable cars now shuttle commuters between the two levels.

lagos.context_blurb: Lagos, on the southwestern coast of Nigeria, is the largest city in Africa, and its population is still exploding — some projections make it the biggest city on Earth before this century is over. It sprawls across a long coastal lagoon in a tangle of islands, bridges, markets, and makeshift waterside settlements. It is a cultural powerhouse: 'Afrobeats' pop and Nollywood films, now a global presence, were both born here.

lahore-the-mughal-city-of-mosque-and-gar.context_blurb: Lahore, in modern Pakistan, was for a long stretch the most important city of the Mughal Empire alongside Delhi and Agra. Many of its emperors preferred it. Within the old city stand some of the great monuments of Mughal architecture: a huge fort, formal pleasure gardens laid out in the Persian style, and one of the largest mosques of the Islamic world, all built in the red sandstone and white marble that are the signature of their era. Lahore is also a city of poets; many of the most-loved poems of modern Urdu were written here.

lake-baikal.context_blurb: Lake Baikal, in southern Siberia, is the oldest, deepest, and largest-by-volume freshwater lake on Earth. It holds roughly one-fifth of all the unfrozen fresh surface water on the planet — more than all of North America's Great Lakes combined. Its basin is a crack in the Earth's crust that has been slowly widening for about 25 million years, and it is still growing. Baikal is home to many species of fish, seal, and sponge that live nowhere else in the world.

lake-natron.context_blurb: Lake Natron, in the Great Rift Valley of northern Tanzania, is a shallow, extremely alkaline soda lake. Its water comes out of the surrounding volcanic rocks loaded with sodium carbonate, which makes the lake caustic to the touch — stronger than ammonia — and gives it a deep red colour from the salt-loving microbes that thrive in it. The lake is a world-famous breeding site for the lesser flamingo, which eats those same microbes. Dead animals that fall in are sometimes pickled by the alkaline water into eerie mummified postures.

lake-nyos.context_blurb: Lake Nyos, in the mountains of northwestern Cameroon, is a deep volcanic crater lake. In August 1986, carbon dioxide gas seeping up from magma below suddenly erupted out of its depths in a single catastrophic blast. The dense gas poured down the surrounding valleys and silently suffocated roughly 1,700 people and thousands of livestock in nearby villages overnight. In the decades since, engineers have installed vertical pipes to slowly degas the lake and prevent a repeat.

lake-superior-and-the-great-lakes.context_blurb: The Great Lakes of North America — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario — together hold roughly 20% of the world's fresh surface water. Lake Superior alone is the largest freshwater lake on Earth by surface area. The lakes were scooped out by continental ice sheets during the last ice age; they drain east through the St Lawrence River to the Atlantic. For both the United States and Canada they have been crucial transport, fishing, and industrial waterways for two centuries.

lake-tanganyika.context_blurb: Lake Tanganyika, in the East African Rift Valley, is the second-oldest and second-deepest freshwater lake in the world, after only Lake Baikal in Siberia. It stretches for over 670 kilometres along the border of four African countries — Tanzania, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Zambia. Like Baikal, it occupies a long thin crack in a continent that is slowly being pulled apart. Hundreds of species of brightly coloured cichlid fish live in its deep waters, and most of them are found nowhere else.

lake-titicaca.context_blurb: Lake Titicaca straddles the border of Peru and Bolivia high in the Andes Mountains, at over 3,800 metres above sea level. It is the largest freshwater lake in South America by volume and is sometimes called the highest navigable lake in the world. The Uru people live on floating islands built out of totora reeds that grow in the lake. In Andean tradition, the lake is the birthplace of the sun and of the ancestors of the Inca, who stepped out of its waters.

lake-victoria.context_blurb: Lake Victoria is the biggest lake in Africa by surface area and the chief source of the Nile River. It is shared by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. The lake is relatively young and shallow for its size. It is also one of the stage-sets of one of the most dramatic recent biological disasters: the introduction of the Nile perch as a food fish in the 1950s and 60s drove hundreds of the lake's distinctive cichlid species to extinction or near-extinction, in what biologists call the largest vertebrate mass extinction of modern times.

laki-1783-the-fissure-that-starved-a-nat.context_blurb: In the summer of 1783 a long volcanic fissure in southern Iceland called Laki opened up and poured out enormous quantities of lava and poisonous sulphur gases for eight months. About a quarter of Iceland's population died in the subsequent famine as livestock perished and crops failed. The gases drifted south across Europe, blanketing it in a strange hazy fog, poisoning crops, and sickening or killing many thousands of people. The disruption may have contributed to the catastrophic grain shortages that helped set the stage for the French Revolution in 1789.

lalibelas-rock-hewn-churches.context_blurb: In the highlands of northern Ethiopia, the medieval king Lalibela ordered an entire cluster of Christian churches carved out of the solid red rock of the mountainside. They were not built up with stones; they were cut down into the earth, each one a single huge sculpture with a hollow interior, roof included. Carved in the 12th and 13th centuries, the churches of Lalibela are still active places of worship for the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, and Christian pilgrims walk between them along passages dug through the rock itself.

lava-lakes-the-worlds-eternal-fire-pits.context_blurb: A persistent lava lake is a pool of molten rock exposed inside a volcanic crater or vent, continuously replenished from below. They are rare — at any given time only a handful exist on Earth. The best-known are at Erta Ale in Ethiopia, Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mount Erebus in Antarctica, and (intermittently) Kilauea in Hawaii. Looking down into one is probably the single most direct window you can get on the molten interior of our planet.

leshan-giant-buddha.context_blurb: At Leshan in Sichuan, China, where three rivers meet, a Chinese Buddhist monk in the 8th century had the mountainside itself carved into a Buddha. The seated figure is more than 70 metres tall from head to foot — the largest ancient stone Buddha in the world. The project took about ninety years. According to tradition, the sculpting was begun to calm the dangerous rapids where the rivers joined, and tons of carved stone dumped into the current from the works really did change its flow.

lhasa-the-potala-palace-above-the-roof-o.context_blurb: Lhasa is the capital of Tibet, high on a plateau at an elevation that leaves most visitors short of breath. Rising above it on a hill is the Potala Palace, a soaring white-and-red fortress-monastery that was for centuries the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas, the spiritual and (until recent times) temporal leaders of Tibetan Buddhism. The current Dalai Lama has lived in exile in India since 1959. The Jokhang Temple down in the old town is the single holiest site in Tibetan Buddhism.

light-bent-into-an-arc-rainbows-and-the-.context_blurb: A rainbow forms when sunlight bends and reflects inside falling raindrops. White sunlight splits into its separate colours and lines up into a circular arc opposite the Sun — red on the outside, violet on the inside, with every observer actually seeing a slightly different rainbow. On rare occasions moonlight is bright enough to produce the same effect, with much paler colours, which is called a moonbow. Double rainbows have a secondary, dimmer bow outside the primary one, with the order of the colours reversed.

lima.context_blurb: Lima, the capital of Peru, lies in a narrow strip of coastal desert between the Pacific Ocean and the foothills of the Andes. It was founded in 1535 by the Spanish conqueror Francisco Pizarro as the seat of Spain's South American viceroyalty, and for about three centuries it was the richest Spanish colonial city on the Pacific coast. It is one of the driest major cities in the world — annual rainfall is almost zero — but it is kept green by rivers running down from the Andes.

linear-b-and-the-burnt-tablets-of-knosso.context_blurb: Linear B is a Bronze Age script found on clay tablets at Knossos on Crete and at several sites on the Greek mainland. For decades after its discovery nobody knew what language it recorded. In the 1950s a brilliant young English architect named Michael Ventris, working with the classicist John Chadwick, finally cracked it: Linear B turned out to be an early form of Greek, written down roughly a thousand years before Homer. The tablets survived precisely because the palaces that stored them burned down, baking the wet clay inventories into permanence.

lisbon-the-quake-that-shook-the-enlighte.context_blurb: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal, perched on seven steep hills above a great natural harbour on the Atlantic. On the morning of November 1, 1755, All Saints' Day, a massive earthquake — followed by a tsunami and a city-wide fire — levelled much of it and killed tens of thousands of people. The disaster rattled Europe intellectually, inspiring Voltaire's Candide and provoking fierce arguments about the goodness of God and the natural order. The city was rebuilt afterward on a famously orderly geometric grid in the old lower town.

loess-ice-age-dust-builds-a-plateau.context_blurb: Loess is a fine, pale yellow wind-blown dust that was blown off the barren outwash plains in front of ice-age glaciers and deposited downwind in huge thick blankets. It covers large regions of the central United States, central Europe, Ukraine, and above all northern China, where the Loess Plateau is tens of metres deep in it. Loess is extraordinarily fertile, which is one reason these regions have long been agricultural heartlands. It also erodes dramatically into vertical cliffs and gullies when water cuts into it.

london-the-city-on-the-tidal-thames.context_blurb: London, on the River Thames in southern England, began as a Roman trading post, grew into the capital of medieval England, and in the 18th and 19th centuries became the headquarters of a global empire. The Thames right through central London is tidal, which allowed the Royal Navy's sailing ships to come straight up to the docks. London has repeatedly reinvented itself: a great plague in 1665, a great fire in 1666, bombing in the Blitz of 1940-41, and most recently a transformation from grimy post-industrial port into one of the world's financial centres.

luang-prabang.context_blurb: Luang Prabang is a tiny former royal capital of Laos, tucked at the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan rivers in the mountains of the country's north. Its small centre is packed with gilded Buddhist temples and French-colonial shuttered villas on sleepy lanes, and every morning at dawn barefoot saffron-robed monks walk through the streets in a long procession collecting rice from kneeling residents.

machu-picchu.context_blurb: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca royal estate perched on a ridge in the cloud forest high above the Urubamba River in the Peruvian Andes. It is built of beautifully fitted stone terraces and buildings and is thought to have been constructed for the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The Spanish, remarkably, never found it, which is one reason it survived in better shape than most Inca sites. It was brought to international attention by the American explorer Hiram Bingham III in 1911, who was led there by a local farmer.

madagascar-the-isolated-ark.context_blurb: Madagascar is a huge island off the southeast coast of Africa — bigger than France — that broke off from the African mainland tens of millions of years ago and from the Indian subcontinent soon after. In its long isolation, its plants and animals evolved on their own path. Roughly 90% of the species found on Madagascar live nowhere else on Earth, including all the lemurs, the fossa, and bizarre spiky trees like the baobab and the octopus tree. Humans only arrived about two thousand years ago, which is very recent as islands go.

maelstroms-the-seas-great-whirlpools.context_blurb: A maelstrom is a powerful, often permanent whirlpool caused by strong tidal currents being forced through a narrow strait. The most famous ones are off the Lofoten Islands in northern Norway, where strong Atlantic tides race through gaps between the islands and spin up turbulent eddies big enough to pull small boats around. The word itself is Norwegian. Edgar Allan Poe and Jules Verne both wrote tales about them in which seafarers get sucked down into the depths, but real maelstroms, though impressive, do not actually swallow ships.

manaus.context_blurb: Manaus is the largest city deep inside the Amazon rainforest, in Brazil, far up the Amazon River where it meets the Rio Negro. At the end of the 19th century it exploded into a short-lived rubber boom and was briefly one of the wealthiest cities in the world; the rubber barons built a grand pink opera house in the middle of the jungle, imported European marble and chandeliers, and brought over opera companies from Italy. The boom collapsed when rubber seedlings smuggled to Southeast Asia undercut Brazilian prices.

manila-intramuros.context_blurb: Manila, the capital of the Philippines, was founded by the Spanish in 1571 on the shore of Manila Bay. For some 250 years it anchored the Manila Galleon trade — a yearly convoy of Spanish treasure ships that carried silver and goods between Manila and Acapulco in Mexico, linking Asia into the Spanish global empire. At the heart of old Manila stands Intramuros, the stone-walled Spanish colonial quarter. Most of it was flattened during the Battle of Manila in 1945; portions have been restored, portions remain scarred.

mariachi-jalisco-mexico.context_blurb: Mariachi is the traditional Mexican ensemble music that most of the world now hears as the sound of Mexico. It grew up in the state of Jalisco in western Mexico in the 19th century, out of a blend of indigenous, Spanish, and French musical traditions. A typical mariachi group includes violins, trumpets, Spanish guitars, a round-bellied bass guitar (the guitarron), and a small high-pitched guitar (the vihuela), with the musicians dressed in the ornate charro outfit of the Mexican horseman. Mariachi was added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2011.

marrakech.context_blurb: Marrakech, in Morocco, was founded in 1070 at the foot of the Atlas Mountains and became the royal capital of successive medieval Berber dynasties ruling an empire that reached from Spain to Senegal. Its old medina is enclosed by red-earth walls, from which the city takes its nickname 'the Red City.' At its heart lies the Jemaa el-Fnaa, a huge market square that empties out during the day and fills with storytellers, snake charmers, musicians, and food stalls at dusk.

mecca-and-the-valley-of-the-hijaz.context_blurb: Mecca, in the dry Hijaz region of western Saudi Arabia, is the holiest city of Islam. It is the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad in the 6th century and the site of the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine around which Muslim worship is organized. Every observant Muslim who can afford to is expected to make the pilgrimage, the Hajj, to Mecca at least once in their lifetime; several million do so every year during a specific week of the Islamic lunar calendar. The city is closed to non-Muslims.

mediterranean-climate-the-scattered-five.context_blurb: A 'Mediterranean climate' means hot dry summers and mild wet winters, and the surprising thing about it is that it occurs in only five places on Earth. One is the actual Mediterranean basin. The other four are coastal California, central Chile, the Cape region of South Africa, and the south and southwest corners of Australia. These five scattered pockets, each sitting on the western edge of a continent at roughly the same latitude, have independently grown drought-tolerant shrublands with similar silver-grey leaves — and in modern times they have become the world's five great wine-making regions.

megathrust-the-deepest-trenches-and-the-.context_blurb: Where one tectonic plate dives down beneath another, the long fault running along the top of the sinking plate is called a megathrust. These are the biggest active faults on Earth, and they produce the biggest earthquakes. The largest earthquakes ever recorded, including the 1960 magnitude 9.5 Chile quake and the 2011 magnitude 9.1 Tohoku quake off Japan, were megathrust events. Earthquakes on megathrusts can also lift the sea floor by metres in seconds, which is what sets off the biggest tsunamis.

meissen-how-europe-cracked-chinas-porcel.context_blurb: For centuries Europeans paid huge sums to import Chinese porcelain, which they could not reproduce. In 1708, in the small Saxon town of Meissen near Dresden in modern Germany, an alchemist named Johann Friedrich Bottger — reportedly working under threat of death from the local prince — finally cracked the recipe. Meissen became the first porcelain factory outside Asia, and its characteristic crossed-swords mark is one of the oldest trademarks still in use. Within a generation, European porcelain workshops had spread across the continent.

melbourne.context_blurb: Melbourne is a southeastern Australian city on a bay off the Southern Ocean. It exploded during the 1850s gold rush in the state of Victoria and briefly, in the 1880s, was one of the richest cities on Earth, with grand Victorian boulevards to prove it. It is a famously liveable modern city with the largest tram network in the English-speaking world. For a few decades (1901-1927) Melbourne even served as the temporary capital of Australia, until Canberra was ready.

mesa-verde.context_blurb: Mesa Verde, in southwestern Colorado in the United States, preserves the most spectacular cliff-dwellings ever built by the Ancestral Puebloans. Beginning around 1200 CE, people who had been farming on top of the flat mesa began moving into the natural rock shelters in its canyon walls and building elaborate multi-story stone-and-mortar villages tucked under the overhangs. The largest of these, Cliff Palace, has over 150 rooms. The whole mesa was abandoned by about 1300, in a drought-stricken migration whose destination is now the Pueblo villages of the Rio Grande.

mexico-city-tenochtitlan.context_blurb: Mexico City sits in a high mountain valley on top of the ruins of Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztec Empire that Hernan Cortes and his Spanish-and-Tlaxcalan forces conquered in 1521. The Aztec city was built on islands in a vast shallow lake, laced with canals; the Spanish filled in most of the lake and built their colonial capital on top. The soft lake-bed sediments mean that modern Mexico City is slowly sinking in uneven patches, so cathedrals and apartment towers lean at odd angles.

miyajima-the-floating-torii.context_blurb: Miyajima is a small forested island in Japan's Seto Inland Sea, considered one of the three most beautiful views in Japan. On its shore stands a huge vermilion Shinto gate — a torii — that has been painted so many times its wood is now sealed in colour. At high tide the sea comes right up around it, so the gate seems to float on the water. Deer wander freely on the island; traditionally no births, deaths, or farming were permitted on it, to keep it sacred.

mohenjo-daro-and-the-indus-cities.context_blurb: In the Indus River valley of modern Pakistan, archaeologists in the 1920s uncovered the ruins of one of the world's three oldest urban civilizations — alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia. The Indus Valley Civilization flourished around 2600 to 1900 BCE, with planned grid-pattern cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, standardized bricks, and sophisticated drainage. Its people wrote in a script that still has not been deciphered. Why their cities emptied out after about 1900 BCE is one of the great unsolved puzzles of ancient history.

monasteries-in-impossible-places.context_blurb: Religious communities around the world have a persistent habit of building their monasteries in places that are as hard as possible to reach: on cliff tops, on isolated sea rocks, inside sheer canyons. The great meteora monasteries of central Greece sit atop pinnacles of rock, originally reached only by net and rope ladder. The Taktsang Palphug ('Tiger's Nest') in Bhutan clings to a cliff hundreds of metres above the valley floor. These places are usually chosen for both their physical remove from worldly distractions and the sheer wonder of occupying such sites.

monte-alban.context_blurb: Monte Alban is an ancient city built on the artificially flattened top of a mountain in the Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico. It was the capital of the Zapotec civilization from roughly 500 BCE to 750 CE, flourishing in parallel with the Maya further east. Its enormous central plaza is lined with pyramids, palaces, and tombs, including a strange J-shaped observatory oriented to the stars. Carved stone slabs around the site depict rows of mysterious contorted figures that early archaeologists called 'the dancers' and whose real meaning is still argued over.

monterey-bay-kelp-forests.context_blurb: Monterey Bay, on the central Californian coast, is one of the richest marine ecosystems on the North American Pacific coast. A deep underwater canyon reaches almost right up to the shore, pulling cold nutrient-rich water from the depths close to the surface. That nutrient supply feeds enormous underwater kelp forests — great golden-brown fronds of giant kelp that grow upward from the sea floor to the surface, forming a canopy about 30 metres tall. Sea otters, harbour seals, sea lions, and leopard sharks all live among the kelp.

montreal.context_blurb: Montreal is on an island in the St. Lawrence River in the Canadian province of Quebec. It is the largest primarily French-speaking city in the Americas and the second-largest in the French-speaking world after Paris. Founded by the French in 1642, it was conquered by the British in 1760 but kept its French language, Catholic churches, and civil-law system. Below its downtown streets runs an enormous network of underground pedestrian passages linking shops, hotels, and metro stations, built so that Montrealers can survive the long winter without stepping outside.

moraines-the-ridges-of-dumped-rubble.context_blurb: A moraine is a ridge or hummocky expanse of rubble — rocks of every size mixed with sand and clay — that a glacier left behind. 'Terminal moraines' mark the furthest point a glacier reached before it stopped and started melting back. The spine of Long Island in New York, for example, is a terminal moraine from the last ice age. Lateral moraines mark the sides of a glacier's track, and medial moraines run down the middle where two glaciers merged.

moscow.context_blurb: Moscow has been the capital of Russia for most of the last five hundred years. In its exact centre, on a bluff above the Moscow River, stands the Kremlin: a vast walled triangle of cathedrals, palaces, and government buildings that has served as the seat of Russian rulers since the days of Ivan the Terrible. Just outside its walls is Red Square, with the brightly-coloured onion domes of St Basil's Cathedral. Moscow was burned during Napoleon's 1812 invasion, held fast against Hitler in 1941, and ruled by Stalin from the Kremlin for a quarter-century.

mount-everest.context_blurb: Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and Tibet, is the highest point on the Earth's land surface, at about 8,849 metres above sea level. Its summit is in what climbers call 'the death zone' above 8,000 metres, where the air is too thin to sustain life for long. Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and the Sherpa Tenzing Norgay were the first climbers confirmed to reach the top, in 1953; since then thousands have followed in their footsteps, with the mountain growing increasingly commercialized. Hundreds have died on it.

mount-fuji.context_blurb: Mount Fuji, west of Tokyo on the main Japanese island of Honshu, is the highest and most iconic mountain in Japan. It is a nearly perfect, symmetrical, snow-capped volcanic cone, and it has been both climbed by Shinto pilgrims and painted by Japanese artists — Hokusai's famous woodblock series of 'Thirty-Six Views' captures it from every angle — for centuries. It last erupted in 1707. On a clear winter day it can be seen from downtown Tokyo more than a hundred kilometres away.

mount-kailash.context_blurb: Mount Kailash in the far west of Tibet is a sacred mountain for four religions at once — Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and the older Tibetan Bon faith — each with its own tradition about who or what the peak is. Hindus consider it the home of the god Shiva. Pilgrims from all four religions walk the roughly 52-kilometre-long devotional circuit around its base at high altitude, taking a few hard days to do a single lap. The mountain itself has never been climbed; all climbing attempts have been forbidden out of religious reverence.

mount-roraima.context_blurb: Mount Roraima, on the triple border of Venezuela, Brazil, and Guyana, is one of the oldest and strangest mountains on Earth. It is a 'tepui' — a flat-topped, sheer-sided table mountain, the eroded remnant of a once-vast sandstone plateau that is now almost two billion years old. Its summit stands as an isolated plateau in the sky, hundreds of metres above the rainforest around it, with its own species of plants and animals that have evolved in isolation. It inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's novel The Lost World.

mount-st-helens-1980-the-sideways-blast.context_blurb: On May 18, 1980, Mount St Helens in Washington State in the United States erupted in one of the most-studied eruptions in modern history. A huge chunk of the mountain's north face collapsed in a giant landslide, which depressurized the magma inside and triggered a lateral blast that flattened forests over hundreds of square kilometres. Fifty-seven people died, including a volcanologist monitoring the mountain. The eruption left a huge horseshoe-shaped crater and a new generation of American geologists who had seen a major eruption up close.

murano-venices-island-of-glass.context_blurb: Murano is a small island cluster in the lagoon of Venice. In 1291, the Venetian government ordered all of Venice's glassmakers to move their furnaces onto Murano — officially to protect the wooden city from kiln fires, but also to keep the glassmakers (and their trade secrets) under control. The Murano workshops dominated European glassmaking for centuries and invented key techniques of clear 'cristallo' glass, enamelled glass, and millefiori. Workers who tried to leave the island with their skills were sometimes hunted down.

mycenae-the-lion-gate-and-the-cyclopean-.context_blurb: Mycenae, in the hills of mainland Greece, was the stronghold of the warrior kingdoms that fought the Trojan War in legend and the real-life center of a late Bronze Age civilization that spoke an early form of Greek. Its massive stone walls are built from blocks so huge that later Greeks assumed only Cyclopes could have moved them, which is still what archaeologists call this style. The main gate is crowned by a carved relief of two heraldic lions — one of the oldest monumental sculptures in Europe.

nan-madol.context_blurb: Nan Madol is a ruined stone city built on top of a coral reef off the Micronesian island of Pohnpei in the western Pacific. Its people, the Saudeleur dynasty, piled up roughly a hundred artificial islets separated by canals, then stacked them with walls of giant basalt logs — natural columns of volcanic rock quarried elsewhere on the island. It flourished from about 1200 to 1600 CE, is sometimes called 'the Venice of the Pacific,' and nobody is quite sure how its people moved the enormous stones into place.

naples-and-the-bay-of-fire.context_blurb: Naples sits on a famous bay on the southern coast of Italy, in the shadow of Mount Vesuvius — the volcano that destroyed Roman Pompeii in AD 79 and could easily erupt again. Just offshore are the volcanic islands of Capri and Ischia; just inland, beneath the suburbs, lie more volcanic calderas that still shift up and down. Naples is the home of pizza (its margherita is the original), it was once the capital of its own kingdom, and its old centre has one of the densest tangles of medieval and Baroque churches anywhere in Europe.

nara-the-first-capital-and-its-great-bud.context_blurb: Nara was the first permanent capital of Japan, established in 710 CE before the court moved on to Kyoto. In this short, intense period it absorbed Chinese models of statecraft and Buddhist architecture. Today the quiet city houses one of the largest wooden buildings on Earth, the Todai-ji, inside which sits an enormous bronze seated Buddha. Hundreds of tame deer wander Nara's park, bowing politely for the biscuits sold to tourists; in Shinto tradition they are considered messengers of the gods.

nazca-lines.context_blurb: On the dry desert plateau south of Lima, Peru, the Nazca people — ancestors of the later Inca — scraped away the dark surface stones to reveal lighter sand underneath, creating a vast gallery of lines and figures spread across hundreds of square kilometres. Some are enormous stylized animals (a monkey, a hummingbird, a spider, a whale) hundreds of metres long; others are long straight lines running toward distant mountains. They were made between roughly 500 BCE and 500 CE. Because they are so big and so flat, their shapes are only fully visible from the air.

new-orleans.context_blurb: New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718 near the mouth of the Mississippi River on the Gulf of Mexico. Over its history it has been French, Spanish, French again, and American, and that layered inheritance shows in everything from its cuisine (gumbo, jambalaya) to its architecture (wrought-iron balconies in the French Quarter) and its Catholic feast-day traditions (Mardi Gras). Much of the city sits below sea level in a shallow bowl, which made the levee failures of Hurricane Katrina in 2005 so devastating.

new-york-city.context_blurb: New York City, on the Atlantic coast of the United States, grew up around one of the finest natural deep-water harbours in the world, which made it an obvious terminus for immigrant ships and transatlantic trade. Its five boroughs — Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island — together hold over eight million people. In the 20th century it emerged as the largest city of the English-speaking world, the headquarters of global finance and advertising, and the symbol of the United States in a thousand films and TV shows.

new-zealand-and-zealandia-the-drowned-co.context_blurb: Geologists now agree that New Zealand sits on the top of its own continent, called Zealandia or Te Riu-a-Maui. The problem is that about 94% of this continent is under the ocean. Only New Zealand, New Caledonia, and a few scattered islands show above the water as the exposed peaks of a drowned landmass. The real continent extends across huge areas of submerged seafloor. New Zealand is also unusual as one of the last large places humans ever reached; Polynesian voyagers arrived there only about 800 years ago.

newgrange-and-bru-na-boinne-the-solstice.context_blurb: In the green rolling fields of the Boyne Valley in Ireland sits Newgrange, a huge grass-covered dome of a tomb built more than 5,000 years ago — older than the pyramids and older than Stonehenge. A long stone passage leads into a cross-shaped burial chamber at its heart. The whole monument was engineered for one astronomical moment each year: for a few minutes around sunrise on the winter solstice, a shaft of light pierces the passage and lights up the inner chamber.

niagara-falls.context_blurb: Niagara Falls, on the border between the United States and Canada, is actually three waterfalls side by side on the Niagara River between Lakes Erie and Ontario. It is not the tallest nor the widest waterfall in the world, but by sheer volume of water tumbling over the edge, it is among the most powerful on Earth. In its two centuries as a tourist attraction, Niagara has drawn tightrope walkers, barrel-riders, honeymooners, and hydroelectric engineers; much of the river's flow is diverted at night to spin turbines.

norse-runes-and-the-jelling-stones.context_blurb: Runes are the angular alphabetic letters that the Vikings and their Germanic ancestors scratched into stone, bone, and wood from about the 2nd century CE through the Middle Ages. Because they had to be cut with a blade across wood grain, the letter shapes are made of straight lines and avoid horizontal strokes. The great Jelling stones in Denmark, raised in the 10th century by King Harald Bluetooth (the king whose nickname was later borrowed for the wireless technology), carry one of the longest and most important royal inscriptions in the runic alphabet.

ocean-gyres-the-garbage-patch-and-the-sh.context_blurb: A gyre is a huge circular current system in an ocean basin. There are five major ones in the world's oceans, driven by winds and the Earth's rotation. The water at the centre of a gyre tends to rotate slowly and accumulate anything that floats — seaweed, driftwood, and now plastic. The 'Great Pacific Garbage Patch,' between California and Hawaii, is the largest known concentration of ocean plastic debris, and the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic is a huge calm patch of ocean where unique rafts of golden sargassum seaweed drift year after year.

old-sanaa.context_blurb: Sanaa, in the mountains of Yemen, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Its old quarter is a dense pack of tall mud-brick tower houses, several storeys each, their upper floors decorated with fired-brick geometric patterns and bands of white gypsum around the windows. Many of these houses are five or six hundred years old and are still lived in by the same families' descendants. The Yemeni civil war that began in 2015 has heavily damaged parts of this fragile old city.

palenque.context_blurb: Palenque, in the forested hills of Chiapas, southern Mexico, is a classic Maya city that flourished from about 300 to 800 CE. Its elegant limestone temples and palace are among the finest achievements of Maya architecture. In 1952, after years of digging through rubble inside the Temple of the Inscriptions, the Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz discovered a sealed stairway leading down into a hidden crypt beneath the pyramid, which turned out to hold the elaborate tomb of a 7th-century ruler named Pakal the Great.

palmyra.context_blurb: Palmyra was a caravan city at an oasis in the Syrian desert, halfway between the Roman and Persian empires. In the 1st to 3rd centuries CE it grew rich as a middleman on the overland silk routes, and its people built an extraordinary skyline of columns, arches, and tower-tombs in a style mixing Greek, Roman, and Persian ideas. Its most famous ruler was Queen Zenobia, who briefly rebelled against Rome. In the 2010s much of its ancient architecture was deliberately blown up by the terrorist group ISIS, which makes the surviving photographs and reconstructions all the more precious.

pamukkale-and-hierapolis.context_blurb: At Pamukkale ('cotton castle') in southwestern Turkey, hot mineral-rich springs cascade down a hillside and deposit layer upon layer of brilliant white calcium carbonate. The result is a staircase of blindingly white terraces holding pools of warm turquoise water — one of the strangest-looking natural landscapes anywhere. On the plateau at the top sits the ruins of Hierapolis, a Greco-Roman spa city whose people came to bathe in these same waters two thousand years ago.

pangaeas-ghost-how-we-know-the-map-moves.context_blurb: The idea that the continents have shifted around the globe over hundreds of millions of years was once ridiculed. The German meteorologist Alfred Wegener laid out the hypothesis in 1912, pointing out how well the eastern coast of South America fits against the western coast of Africa, and how matching fossils and rock types line up across the ocean. His 'continental drift' idea was dismissed because no one could think of a mechanism. In the 1960s, new data from the sea floor revealed the mechanism, and plate tectonics became scientific consensus.

paris-the-city-above-and-below.context_blurb: Paris, on the River Seine in northern France, has been the capital of France for well over a thousand years. Its skyline above the river is still mostly the one laid out in the great 19th-century redesign by Baron Haussmann, whose boulevards cut long straight lines through the medieval maze. Below the streets runs an immense parallel city of tunnels: Metro lines, sewers, ancient limestone quarries, and the famous ossuary where the bones of several million Parisians were quietly moved in the 1780s when the city's cemeteries overflowed.

perito-moreno-glacier-patagonia.context_blurb: The Perito Moreno Glacier, in the Argentine Patagonia on the border with Chile, is one of the most accessible large glaciers on Earth. Walkways let visitors stand right in front of a sheer blue ice wall nearly 60 metres high, where huge slabs of ice regularly crack off and crash into the lake below. Unlike most of the world's glaciers today, Perito Moreno is roughly stable in size, neither clearly advancing nor clearly retreating. Every few years its advancing snout dams a nearby lake, the water builds up behind it, and finally the ice bridge spectacularly collapses in a cycle locals have been watching for decades.

permafrost-and-siberias-frozen-ground.context_blurb: Permafrost is soil that has stayed frozen year-round for at least two consecutive years; much of it has been frozen for tens of thousands of years. It underlies about a quarter of the land in the Northern Hemisphere, mostly in Siberia, Canada, and Alaska. Enormous amounts of ancient organic matter — mammoth bones, grass, soil carbon — are locked up in it. Siberia has recently produced extraordinary intact remains of ice-age animals, including woolly rhinos and cave lions, released as the permafrost begins to thaw.

persepolis.context_blurb: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the ancient Persian Empire of Darius and Xerxes, built on a huge stone terrace in the mountains of modern Iran. Its stairways are carved with endless reliefs of tribute-bearers from all 23 nations of the empire, each wearing their own costumes and bringing their own gifts. In 330 BCE Alexander the Great captured the city and allowed his troops to burn it down. The columns and gateways still stand where fire scorched them 2,300 years ago.

persian-carpets-irans-woven-gardens.context_blurb: The weaving of knotted-pile wool carpets has been practised in what is now Iran for more than two thousand years. Persian carpets are famous for their almost impossibly fine knot counts and for their complex floral and garden designs, which deliberately depict Paradise as a watered garden seen from above. Centres of weaving — Tabriz, Kashan, Isfahan, Qom — each have their own regional patterns and colour palettes. The finest antique Persian carpets today sell at auction for millions of dollars.

petra.context_blurb: Hidden in a steep red-rock canyon in southern Jordan lies Petra, the ancient capital of the Nabataeans — a desert trading people who grew wealthy controlling the frankincense and spice caravans. Carved directly into the sandstone cliffs are elaborate temple and tomb facades, the most famous reached by walking down a narrow natural gorge that suddenly opens onto an immense pink facade. The Nabataeans were master water engineers who could support a city of tens of thousands in the middle of the desert. Petra was lost to the outside world for centuries before a Swiss explorer rediscovered it in 1812.

pinatubo-1991-the-eruption-that-cooled-t.context_blurb: In June 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted in one of the biggest volcanic blasts of the 20th century. Thanks to careful forecasting by Filipino and American geologists, hundreds of thousands of people were evacuated in time and relatively few died. The eruption injected huge quantities of sulphur-dioxide into the stratosphere, forming a sulphate-aerosol haze that reflected sunlight. For the next two years average global temperatures dropped measurably — a brief, natural real-world test of how volcanic aerosols can cool the climate.

pingyao-the-frozen-ming-city.context_blurb: Pingyao is a walled city in Shanxi province, central China, with the best-preserved Ming- and Qing-era streetscape of any town in the country. In the 19th century it was the birthplace of modern Chinese banking — the first bank-draft houses were founded here — but then the trade moved to the coast, Pingyao stagnated, and in stagnating it accidentally saved itself. While most other Chinese cities were torn down and rebuilt during the 20th century, Pingyao kept its narrow lanes, courtyard houses, and city walls more or less intact.

pisa-the-tower-that-sank-as-it-rose.context_blurb: Pisa is a modest Italian city on the Arno River, between Florence and the Mediterranean coast. It was once a wealthy maritime republic. Today most visitors come to see one building: a slender white marble bell-tower that began to tilt during its own construction in the 12th century, when its foundations settled unevenly on the soft ground. For centuries it leaned more and more precariously; recent engineering has stabilized it at a safe angle that preserves its famous crooked silhouette.

polynesian-wayfinding.context_blurb: Polynesian wayfinding is the lost-and-recovered art by which the ancestors of modern Hawaiians, Maori, Samoans, and Tahitians sailed thousands of kilometres across the open Pacific — without compasses, maps, or metal tools — and found every habitable island in the world's largest ocean. They used stars, swell patterns, cloud shapes, the behaviour of seabirds, and the feel of the sea itself. Western scholars long thought such feats impossible until, in the late 20th century, voyages like that of the double-hulled canoe Hokule'a sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti and back using only traditional navigation.

pompeii-and-herculaneum-frozen-by-vesuvi.context_blurb: In AD 79 the volcano Vesuvius, on the Bay of Naples in Italy, erupted catastrophically and buried the two Roman towns at its foot — Pompeii and Herculaneum — under metres of hot ash and pumice. For 1,700 years the towns lay forgotten. When excavation finally began in the 18th century, archaeologists discovered that the eruption had sealed in everything: shops with loaves still on the counters, graffiti, political slogans, even the hollow shapes of the victims themselves, which could be re-cast in plaster. No other Roman city gives such an unbroken window into ordinary daily life.

potosi.context_blurb: The town of Potosi, in the Bolivian Andes, sits at over 4,000 metres above sea level at the foot of a reddish conical peak called Cerro Rico ('Rich Mountain'). For about two hundred years after the Spanish began mining it in the 1540s, this one mountain produced the staggering bulk of the silver that flowed from the Americas to Spain and reshaped the global economy. The Spanish forced indigenous people and enslaved Africans to work in its mines in horrifying conditions. The phrase 'worth a Potosi' entered Spanish as a measure of unimaginable wealth.

prague.context_blurb: Prague, the capital of the Czech Republic, straddles the Vltava River in the heart of Central Europe. Because it was spared the heavy bombing of World War II, its old centre survives as a continuous textbook of European architecture — Gothic cathedrals, Renaissance palaces, Baroque churches, Art Nouveau — all layered on medieval street plans. For six centuries from the 10th to the early 20th, Prague was a major capital of the Holy Roman Empire and later the Habsburg monarchy, and its Jewish quarter is one of the oldest in Europe.

prambanan.context_blurb: Not far from Borobudur, on the island of Java in Indonesia, stands the 9th-century Hindu temple complex of Prambanan: a cluster of towering, slender stone spires honouring the gods Shiva, Vishnu, and Brahma. Although Indonesia today is overwhelmingly Muslim, Java was once a great centre of Hindu-Buddhist civilization, and Prambanan is one of the largest Hindu temples in Southeast Asia. Its walls are carved with scenes from the Ramayana, which are still performed as a dance-drama in front of the temple on moonlit nights.

quebec-city.context_blurb: Quebec City, in eastern Canada, is one of the oldest European-founded cities in North America — established by Samuel de Champlain in 1608 on a dramatic cliff overlooking the narrows of the St. Lawrence River. The historic quarter atop the cliff is still enclosed by the only surviving stone fortifications of any walled city north of Mexico. The city is defiantly French-speaking: it is the capital of the province of Quebec, which has twice held referendums on seceding from Canada.

rain-shadow-deserts-the-dry-side-of-the-.context_blurb: A rain-shadow desert forms on the leeward side of a mountain range. Prevailing moist air is forced upward by the mountains, cools, and drops its rain on the windward slopes. By the time the air descends on the other side it is dry. Death Valley is dry because of the Sierra Nevada; the Patagonian desert because of the Andes; the Gobi because of the Himalayas; the Negev because of the mountains of the Levant. Rain shadows explain many of the world's biggest deserts.

reggae-ska-and-dub-kingston-jamaica.context_blurb: In the 1960s and 70s, the small island of Jamaica produced an outsized cluster of popular music genres that reshaped global pop. Ska came first, out of the sound-system DJ culture of Kingston, drawing on American jazz and rhythm-and-blues. Rocksteady slowed it down. Reggae — identified above all with Bob Marley and the Wailers — slowed it further and infused it with Rastafarian spirituality and social protest. Dub, pioneered by producers like King Tubby and Lee Perry, stripped reggae tracks down to their rhythmic bones and layered on heavy reverb and echo.

reykjavik.context_blurb: Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland, is the northernmost capital of an independent country in the world, sitting just a few degrees south of the Arctic Circle. Although it only became a proper town in the 18th century, its name — meaning 'smoky bay' — refers to the steam rising from geothermal hot springs that the first Viking settlers saw as they came ashore. Those same hot springs now heat virtually every house in the city. Iceland sits on top of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where two tectonic plates pull apart, which is also why the ground around Reykjavik is so volcanically restless.

rio-de-janeiro.context_blurb: Rio de Janeiro, on the Atlantic coast of Brazil, has one of the most spectacular natural settings of any big city on Earth: steep granite peaks (Sugar Loaf, Corcovado) rising straight out of a tropical blue bay, with long white beaches wrapped around the base. From the summit of Corcovado an enormous Art Deco statue of Christ the Redeemer looks down over the city. Rio was the capital of Brazil until 1960, when the government moved inland to the newly built Brasilia; it remains the heart of Brazilian carnival culture.

river-deltas-where-a-river-drops-its-loa.context_blurb: A delta is a landform built up where a river slows down as it meets the sea, lake, or other still body of water, and drops the sediment it has been carrying downstream. The classic triangular shape (which gave the Greek letter delta its name) was first noticed by Greek observers of the Nile. Deltas are usually extremely fertile and heavily populated — the Ganges, Mississippi, Nile, Mekong, Rhine-Meuse, and Yangtze deltas each support tens of millions of people, often at risk from storms, floods, and sea-level rise.

rome-the-eternal-citys-engineering.context_blurb: Rome, the capital of modern Italy, was for roughly five hundred years the capital of an empire that stretched from Scotland to Mesopotamia. The modern city is layered on top of that ancient one: a Renaissance church sits inside a Roman temple here, a medieval tower rises from the stump of a Roman theatre there. In the middle of Rome is Vatican City, the independent state that is the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church, with its own basilica, museums, and (though they rarely draw their swords) its own Swiss Guard.

rongorongo-the-lost-script-of-easter-isl.context_blurb: Rongorongo is a mysterious script found carved into wooden tablets by the people of Easter Island (Rapa Nui) in the remote southeastern Pacific. It is one of only a handful of writing systems that may have been invented independently in human history. By the time 19th-century missionaries noticed the tablets, the people who could read them were already dead — many killed by Peruvian slave raids and introduced disease — and only a few dozen tablets survive. Modern scholars have tried for over a century to decipher the script, mostly without success.

rotorua.context_blurb: Rotorua is a town in the North Island of New Zealand, famous for being built right on top of an active geothermal field. The whole place smells of sulphur. Hot pools bubble in people's back gardens, geysers go off a short walk from the town centre, and heated mud boils in roadside parks. It is also one of the heartlands of Maori culture — the local iwi have lived with and used these hot springs for centuries, and tourists come as much for traditional Maori hospitality as for the geology.

ryoan-ji-kyotos-garden-of-stone.context_blurb: Ryoan-ji is a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan, whose rock garden is one of the most famous works of art in the Japanese tradition. The garden is a rectangle of raked white gravel in which fifteen stones are placed, arranged in groups, with nothing else — no plants, no water. No matter where you stand to look at it, at least one of the fifteen stones is always hidden from view. It was laid out in the 15th century, and nobody is quite sure what, if anything, it is meant to represent.

salar-de-uyuni.context_blurb: The Salar de Uyuni, in the high Andes of Bolivia, is the world's largest salt flat — an almost perfectly flat expanse of white salt stretching to the horizon in every direction. It is the dry bed of a huge ancient lake. For a few months of the year a thin layer of water from the surrounding mountains covers it, turning the whole salar into a vast natural mirror reflecting the sky. The Salar also holds an enormous share of the world's known lithium reserves, locked up in brine beneath the salt crust.

samarkand-the-registan-and-timurs-blue-c.context_blurb: Samarkand, in modern Uzbekistan, was one of the glittering cities of the medieval Silk Road and the capital of the 14th-century conqueror Timur (Tamerlane). Timur deported the best craftsmen from the lands he sacked and set them to work beautifying his city. The result is one of the most dazzling pieces of Islamic architecture anywhere on Earth: a central square called the Registan ringed on three sides by huge madrasas whose facades are entirely covered in intricate turquoise and blue tile mosaics.

samba-and-bossa-nova-rio-de-janeiro.context_blurb: Samba is the national dance of Brazil, born in the early 20th century in the working-class and Afro-Brazilian neighbourhoods of Rio de Janeiro from African, Portuguese, and Brazilian folk roots. It became the heart of Rio's famous Carnival parades. In the late 1950s a sophisticated, quieter cousin of samba, called bossa nova, was born in the beach-side apartments of Ipanema and Copacabana. Musicians like Antonio Carlos Jobim, Joao Gilberto, and the poet Vinicius de Moraes crossed samba's rhythms with cool jazz harmonies — the result was 'The Girl from Ipanema' and a whole quietly cosmopolitan Brazilian sound.

san-francisco.context_blurb: San Francisco sits on a hilly peninsula on the Pacific coast of California at the mouth of a vast bay. It leapt into existence as a boom town during the 1849 California Gold Rush and has repeatedly reinvented itself since: as the great Pacific port of its day, as the city flattened and rebuilt after the enormous 1906 earthquake, as the capital of the 1960s counterculture, and in our own era as the headquarters of Silicon Valley's internet companies. The Golden Gate Bridge spans the mouth of the bay in a dramatic sweep of orange steel.

santorini-the-caldera-behind-the-atlanti.context_blurb: The Greek island of Santorini, in the Aegean, is actually the ragged rim of a sunken volcanic crater. In roughly 1600 BCE the volcano exploded catastrophically, blowing out its own middle and leaving behind the horseshoe-shaped island cluster we see today. The eruption may have contributed to the decline of the Minoan civilization on nearby Crete and is often suggested as the historical kernel of Plato's story of Atlantis — the island civilization that supposedly disappeared beneath the sea in a day and a night.

seoul-palace-city-on-the-worlds-stranges.context_blurb: Seoul has been the capital of Korea for most of the last 600 years. In 1950 it changed hands four times during the Korean War, which left the Korean peninsula split in two by a cease-fire line only a short drive north of the city. Seoul rebuilt itself from the ruins and became one of the wealthiest, most technologically advanced cities in Asia. Its old royal palaces — courtyards and tiled roofs restored after years of Japanese demolition — sit in the shadow of glass skyscrapers.

sequoyah-and-the-cherokee-syllabary.context_blurb: Sequoyah was a Cherokee silversmith in the early 1800s who had never learned to read or write any language. He became fascinated with the idea that the words of the English-speaking white settlers around him could be captured on paper, and he set out to produce the same gift for his own people's language. Working alone over several years, he devised a 'syllabary' — a set of about 86 symbols, each standing for one Cherokee syllable — and the Cherokee Nation officially adopted it in 1825. Within a few years Cherokee literacy rates were higher than those of their white neighbours.

serabit-el-khadim-the-alphabet-born-in-a.context_blurb: At Serabit el-Khadim, a remote Egyptian turquoise mine on the Sinai Peninsula, archaeologists have found strange rock-cut inscriptions in a very early script, dating to roughly 1800 BCE. The signs look like simplified Egyptian hieroglyphs, but they are being used for a Semitic language — the ancestors of Hebrew, Aramaic, and Phoenician. Many scholars now think these 'Proto-Sinaitic' inscriptions represent the earliest known step toward the alphabet, probably invented by Semitic-speaking workers at the mines who had seen Egyptian writing and simplified it for their own tongue.

seville-the-inland-gate-to-the-americas.context_blurb: Seville, in southern Spain, is the capital of Andalusia and the fourth-largest city in the country. It sits on the Guadalquivir River, far enough inland that a sailing ship can only just reach it on the tide. In the 16th century, that geography put Seville in a monopoly position: for about two hundred years, every ship travelling between Spain and its new empire in the Americas had to pass through its port. The city grew spectacularly wealthy, which paid for its enormous Gothic cathedral and its elegant royal palace, the Alcazar.

shanghai-the-bund-facing-the-future.context_blurb: Shanghai sits on the Yangtze River delta on the east coast of China. In the 19th and early 20th centuries it was carved up into foreign-controlled 'concessions' and became a cosmopolitan port lined with grand European-style banks along the river — the famous 'Bund.' After 1949 it was austerely closed off; from the 1990s onwards it has exploded into one of the great global financial cities, with a forest of skyscrapers rising on what used to be marsh across the river from the Bund.

shibam.context_blurb: Shibam is a small walled town in the Hadramawt valley of Yemen, famous as 'the Manhattan of the desert.' Within its mud-brick walls stand several hundred tower-houses, some rising up to eight or eleven stories, all built packed tight together on a tight grid plan. It is widely considered the oldest skyscraper city in the world. Most of the current buildings are a few hundred years old, though they stand on much older foundations.

shwedagon-pagoda-yangon.context_blurb: The Shwedagon Pagoda, in the heart of Yangon in Myanmar, is the holiest Buddhist site in the country. It is a single enormous gilded stupa — a solid conical mountain of brickwork sheathed in real gold leaf — rising from a hilltop and ringed by smaller shrines. The structure has been renovated and re-gilded by successive Burmese kings over the centuries; its very topmost tip is set with a single large diamond. Devotees walk clockwise around the pagoda making offerings.

sigiriya.context_blurb: Sigiriya in central Sri Lanka is an isolated plug of volcanic rock rising abruptly about 180 metres above the surrounding plain. In the late 5th century CE, King Kashyapa fortified its summit and built himself a palace up there, approached by a staircase that passed between the paws of a colossal carved lion gatehouse. Partway up the cliff, under a sheltering overhang, are a series of frescoes of celestial maidens that are among the oldest surviving Sri Lankan paintings.

silk-chinas-two-thousand-year-secret.context_blurb: Silk is a shining, strong textile fibre spun by the caterpillars of certain moths. Chinese tradition says it was discovered around 2700 BCE by the empress Leizu, and for roughly two thousand years China kept the technique for making it a jealously guarded state secret. Caravans travelled westward from China all the way to Rome carrying bolts of the finished cloth — the famous Silk Road is named for this traffic — while the actual silkworms, their eggs, and the mulberry leaves they ate stayed inside China. The secret eventually leaked out via Korea, Japan, and India.

singapore.context_blurb: Singapore is a small city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, sitting on one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world. It was founded as a British trading post by Stamford Raffles in 1819, became briefly independent in 1965 after being expelled from the Malaysian federation, and under the long rule of Lee Kuan Yew transformed itself from a scrappy port into one of the wealthiest and most tightly-managed cities in the world. Famously orderly, it is also one of the few islands of English Common Law in Southeast Asia.

skara-brae-and-neolithic-orkney.context_blurb: On a windswept beach of the Orkney Islands north of Scotland sits Skara Brae, the best-preserved Stone Age village in all of northern Europe. Built around 3100 BCE and buried by sand for most of the next five thousand years, its stone houses still have their original stone dressers, bed-frames, and hearths standing in place. A great storm in 1850 stripped the sand away and revealed it. The village is older than Stonehenge and older than the Egyptian pyramids.

st-petersburg.context_blurb: St Petersburg was founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703 on a boggy stretch of the Baltic coast in the far northwest of Russia, explicitly as a modern 'window on the West.' Peter forced his aristocrats to move there, build Italian- and French-style palaces, and reorient Russia's culture toward Europe. The city served as the capital of the Russian Empire for two centuries. During World War II it endured the brutal 872-day Siege of Leningrad, in which something like a million civilians died.

stockholm.context_blurb: Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, is built on fourteen islands at the point where Lake Malaren meets the Baltic Sea, giving it a strikingly watery, maritime character. Sweden has not fought a war in over two hundred years, which has let Stockholm's old town — the Gamla Stan — survive intact as one of the best-preserved medieval city centres in northern Europe. The city is also where the Nobel Prizes are awarded each December.

stone-town-zanzibar.context_blurb: Stone Town is the old quarter of Zanzibar City on the island of Zanzibar, off the Tanzanian coast. For centuries the island was a crossroads where African, Arab, Indian, and European cultures mixed: it was ruled by sultans of Oman, who grew rich on cloves and (less creditably) on the slave trade. Its tall coral-stone houses are famous for carved wooden doors, each a signature of the family that lived behind it. The singer Freddie Mercury of Queen was born here.

stonehenge-salisbury-plain.context_blurb: On the chalk downs of southern England stands Stonehenge: a ring of enormous standing stones, some topped with horizontal lintels locked in place like Lego. It was built in stages between roughly 3000 and 1500 BCE by Neolithic and early Bronze Age people whose names we will never know. The site is aligned to the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Where some of the stones came from, how they were moved tens or hundreds of kilometres, and what the whole thing was for are all still mysteries that archaeologists argue about.

summits-left-unclimbed-out-of-reverence.context_blurb: A handful of mountains around the world have been deliberately left unclimbed in modern times out of respect for the local people who hold them sacred. Mount Kailash in Tibet is one. The entire peak of Gangkhar Puensum in Bhutan — technically the highest unclimbed mountain on Earth — is off-limits by Bhutanese government decree. Mount Machapuchare in Nepal, Mount Kawagarbo in Yunnan, and others also carry no-climb policies. These are deliberate choices to preserve the religious meaning of a place.

svalbard-and-the-global-seed-vault.context_blurb: Svalbard is a cold Norwegian archipelago high in the Arctic Ocean, about halfway between mainland Norway and the North Pole. It is one of the northernmost places on Earth with permanent settlements. Buried in a mountainside on one of its islands sits the Global Seed Vault — a huge refrigerated backup library of over a million distinct crop varieties from every country on Earth, meant to safeguard the world's agricultural diversity against regional catastrophes. The vault is often called 'the doomsday vault.'

sydney.context_blurb: Sydney, on the southeastern coast of Australia, grew up around one of the great natural deep-water harbours of the world. It was founded as a British penal colony in 1788; today it is Australia's largest and most populous city. Its skyline is defined by two neighbouring icons on the harbour: a steel arch bridge from 1932 and a white-sailed opera house from 1973. The surrounding beaches, inlets, and sandstone cliffs make it one of the most spectacularly-sited cities in the Southern Hemisphere.

ta-prohm.context_blurb: Ta Prohm is one of the temples of the Angkor complex in Cambodia, built in the 12th century as a Buddhist monastery. When the French began restoring Angkor in the early 20th century, they decided to leave this one almost as they found it: half-swallowed by jungle, with enormous silk-cotton and strangler-fig trees growing on top of the stone galleries, roots prising apart the walls. It is the picture people usually have in mind when they imagine a jungle-eaten lost temple, and it was used as a setting for the first Tomb Raider film.

taj-mahal.context_blurb: The Taj Mahal, on the banks of the Yamuna River in Agra, India, is a vast white-marble mausoleum completed in 1653. It was ordered by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth. The whole structure is laid out as a huge symmetrical garden-tomb, with reflecting pools, calligraphy, and inlaid semi-precious stones; the marble subtly changes colour through the day. It is widely considered one of the most beautiful buildings ever built.

tallinn.context_blurb: Tallinn, on the Baltic Sea, is the capital of Estonia and once one of the northernmost outposts of the Hanseatic League of medieval trading cities. Its upper and lower towns, both protected by stone walls studded with round defensive towers, together make up one of the best-preserved medieval walled cities in all of northern Europe. Tallinn is unexpectedly famous in another dimension: in the two decades since Estonia regained independence from the Soviet Union, it has become one of Europe's most digitally advanced cities, home of Skype's original engineering team and a model for e-government.

tambora-and-the-year-without-a-summer.context_blurb: In April 1815, Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa exploded in what geologists call the largest volcanic eruption in recorded human history. Tens of thousands of people in the vicinity were killed outright. The volcano hurled vast amounts of sulphur into the stratosphere, and the following year — 1816 — summers across the Northern Hemisphere were brutally cold. New England and Europe got frost and snow in June and July. Crops failed, food prices rose, and a group of friends on a lakeside holiday in Switzerland, kept indoors by the weird weather, wrote the ghost stories that produced both Frankenstein and the first modern vampire tale.

tartan-and-the-kilt-highland-scotland.context_blurb: The patterned woollen cloth known as tartan has been woven in the Scottish Highlands for many centuries. Specific colour and stripe combinations — the 'setts' — were traditionally associated with particular regions and later with specific Highland clans. The pleated knee-length wool wrap known as the kilt is a somewhat later development that reached its modern form in the 18th century. Both tartan and the kilt were briefly banned in Scotland after the Jacobite uprising of 1745, as a tool for suppressing Highland identity. The ban was repealed, and tartan has flourished ever since.

temperate-rainforests-the-cool-wet-giant.context_blurb: The world has two very different kinds of rainforest. The famous tropical ones straddle the equator; the temperate ones hug the cool, foggy, mountainous west coasts of the mid-latitudes. The best-known temperate rainforests run along the Pacific coast of North America from northern California up into Alaska. Others grow in southern Chile, in Tasmania and New Zealand, and in a thin strip of coastal Norway. Their rain is so steady that the branches of the vast evergreens — redwoods, Sitka spruce, Douglas firs — are drooping with mosses and lichens.

tenochtitlan.context_blurb: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, founded around 1325 on islands in a shallow lake in the Valley of Mexico. By the early 16th century it was one of the biggest cities in the world, with grand pyramid-temples, canals, floating gardens, and causeways connecting it to the mainland. When Hernan Cortes and his small Spanish force arrived in 1519 they were astonished by what they saw. Within two years they had conquered the city, in alliance with Aztec rivals, and begun building modern Mexico City on top of its ruins.

teotihuacan.context_blurb: Teotihuacan, in the Valley of Mexico north of modern Mexico City, was one of the biggest cities in the ancient world. At its height around 500 CE it had somewhere around 125,000 people, making it bigger than any city in Europe at the time. Its planned grid of streets is dominated by two massive pyramids — the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon — along the central 'Avenue of the Dead.' We do not know what the builders called themselves. The city was already a mysterious ruin to the later Aztecs, who gave it the name it still bears.

the-aksum-obelisks-stelae-of-axum.context_blurb: In the ancient Ethiopian city of Aksum stand some of the tallest single blocks of stone ever quarried and raised anywhere on Earth. Carved more than 1,700 years ago by the Christian kingdom of Aksum, they are tall granite pillars sculpted to look like multi-storey buildings, with rows of 'windows' and 'doors' incised into their faces. The largest one lies broken on the ground; it probably collapsed during the attempt to raise it. One of the others was carried off by Mussolini's troops in 1937 and only returned to Ethiopia in the 2000s.

the-alps.context_blurb: The Alps are the great mountain range of central Europe, arcing across parts of France, Italy, Switzerland, Germany, Austria, and Slovenia. They were pushed up by the slow collision of the African tectonic plate with Europe, and that collision is still going on. Their famous peaks — the Matterhorn, Mont Blanc, the Eiger — have been the training ground for mountaineering for two centuries. The Alps are also the water tower of Europe: four of the continent's main rivers (the Rhine, the Rhone, the Danube, and the Po) rise in them.

the-amazon.context_blurb: The Amazon, in South America, is the largest river in the world by volume: it carries about one-fifth of all the freshwater running into the oceans. By length it is a very close second to the Nile. Its drainage basin covers an area roughly the size of the continental United States and is dominated by the Amazon rainforest, home to a staggering fraction of all the species on Earth. The river rises in the Andes and runs more than 6,000 kilometres east across Brazil to the Atlantic Ocean.

the-andes.context_blurb: The Andes form the longest mountain range on dry land, running for roughly 7,000 kilometres down the entire western edge of South America from Venezuela to Patagonia. They were raised by the slow forcing of the Pacific plate down under the South American plate; both the subduction and the uplift are still active, which is why the range is studded with volcanoes and earthquakes. The Inca built their empire among the Andes, and today their towns and cities hold the highest capital, the highest navigable lake, and some of the highest permanently inhabited settlements in the world.

the-appalachians.context_blurb: The Appalachian Mountains run for about 2,400 kilometres down the eastern side of North America, from Canada to Alabama. In their youth, several hundred million years ago, they were as high as the Himalayas; today they are a long chain of wooded, rounded, deeply eroded ridges and valleys. They form a line that European settlers struggled to cross for the first century of American colonization. Geologically, parts of them line up with mountain ranges in Scotland and Morocco, which were all once part of the same single range before the Atlantic Ocean opened and split them apart.

the-aral-sea.context_blurb: The Aral Sea, straddling the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in Central Asia, was once the fourth-largest inland body of water in the world. In the 1960s, Soviet planners diverted the two rivers that fed it to irrigate cotton fields across the surrounding desert. The lake shrank catastrophically. Today most of its old basin is dry salt desert; rusting fishing boats sit stranded in the sand kilometres from any water. It is widely considered one of the worst human-caused ecological disasters ever recorded. The northern remnant has been partially restored.

the-arctic-ocean-and-the-north-pole.context_blurb: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of Earth's oceans, surrounded on nearly all sides by the land of North America, Europe, and Asia. For most of history it has been covered by a layer of floating sea ice. The geographic North Pole sits in the middle of this ice — there is no land under it, only ocean — which is why reaching the pole has traditionally meant trekking across drifting ice floes. The Arctic sea ice has been visibly shrinking over recent decades as the climate warms.

the-atacama.context_blurb: The Atacama Desert runs for a thousand kilometres along the coast of northern Chile between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes. It is one of the driest places on Earth: parts of it have gone decades at a stretch without recording measurable rain. The combination of extreme dryness and high altitude also gives the Atacama some of the clearest night skies in the world, which is why many of the world's largest telescopes are built there.

the-atacama-the-driest-place-on-earth.context_blurb: The Atacama Desert of northern Chile is widely considered the driest desert on Earth. Some weather stations in it have never recorded rainfall. Its extraordinary dryness comes from a combination of three factors: it sits on the leeward side of the Andes in a rain shadow; it also sits on the warm leeward side of the coastal range along the Pacific; and offshore the cold Humboldt Current stabilizes the air and discourages storms. NASA uses it to simulate conditions on Mars.

the-bagpipes-contested-home.context_blurb: The bagpipes are one of the oldest wind-instrument families on Earth; variants on them are found from Scotland to Pakistan. The world most strongly associates them with the Scottish Highlands, where the Great Highland Bagpipe has been a battle instrument of Scottish regiments for centuries. But bagpipe-type instruments were played throughout the ancient Mediterranean and have been found at Hadrian's Wall; versions appear in Spanish Galicia, Bulgaria, Ireland, and across the Balkans. The question 'where were bagpipes invented?' turns out to be surprisingly hard to answer.

the-bay-of-fundy-highest-tides-on-earth.context_blurb: The Bay of Fundy, between the Canadian provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, has the highest tides anywhere on Earth. Twice a day the water level at its head rises and falls by over 15 metres — about the height of a four-storey building — in roughly six hours. The reason is a lucky accident of basin geometry: the natural slosh period of the bay happens to be about the same as the twice-daily tidal cycle, so each tide reinforces the next. At low tide, people walk out on sea floor that was underwater six hours earlier.

the-bering-land-bridge-beringia.context_blurb: During the last Ice Age so much of the Earth's water was locked up in continental ice sheets that global sea level stood more than a hundred metres below where it is today. In that time, Alaska and eastern Siberia were connected by a vast exposed plain of grassland rather than a narrow sea strait. Geneticists and archaeologists agree that this corridor, called Beringia, is how the ancestors of the Native American peoples first crossed from Asia into the Americas, probably in several waves between about 25,000 and 15,000 years ago.

the-blues-the-mississippi-delta.context_blurb: The blues was born in the Mississippi Delta region of the American Deep South, among African-American sharecroppers and labourers in the decades after the Civil War. Rooted in work songs, spirituals, and West African musical traditions, it developed a distinctive vocabulary of twelve-bar progressions, 'blue' flattened notes, and lyrics structured around repeated lines. From the Delta, singers like Robert Johnson, Charley Patton, and Son House carried the music up the Mississippi to Memphis and Chicago, where electrified versions evolved and eventually fed into rock and roll.

the-camino-de-santiago.context_blurb: The Camino de Santiago is the medieval Christian pilgrimage route that ends at the shrine of the apostle Saint James in the city of Santiago de Compostela, in Galicia in northwestern Spain. The best-known branch is the Camino Frances, a roughly 800-kilometre walking route that crosses the Pyrenees from France and traverses northern Spain. The pilgrimage dates to the 9th century, became one of the great devotions of medieval Europe, and has been massively revived in recent decades by both religious and secular walkers.

the-caspian-sea.context_blurb: The Caspian Sea, bordered by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, and Azerbaijan, is the largest completely enclosed body of water on Earth — depending on how you draw the categories, it is either the biggest lake in the world or an inland sea in its own right. It is a leftover of the vast ancient ocean that once stretched across what is now central Eurasia. Its water is brackish, somewhere between fresh and sea water. Its basin holds enormous reserves of oil and natural gas and is the natural home of the beluga sturgeon, whose roe is the source of the most expensive caviar.

the-colosseum-romes-flavian-amphitheatre.context_blurb: The Colosseum, in the middle of modern Rome, is the largest amphitheatre ever built in the ancient Roman world. It was completed in AD 80 and could seat somewhere around 50,000 spectators for gladiator fights, mock sea-battles, and animal spectacles. Beneath its arena floor is a maze of chambers and lifts where gladiators and wild beasts waited to be hoisted up into view. Even half-ruined and stripped of its marble, it is still the biggest standing Roman building and the icon of Rome itself.

the-congo.context_blurb: The Congo River, in central Africa, is the second-longest river in Africa after the Nile and by volume second only to the Amazon anywhere in the world. It is unusual for crossing the equator twice on its long bending path through the rainforest. The Congo basin holds the second-largest tropical rainforest on Earth. Downstream of the modern cities of Kinshasa and Brazzaville, the river tumbles through the Livingstone Falls on its way to the Atlantic — a series of rapids so violent that the river is unnavigable by boat for its last few hundred kilometres.

the-coriolis-effect-why-the-storms-spin.context_blurb: Because the Earth is rotating, anything moving freely over its surface for a long time appears to curve, from the point of view of someone standing on the ground. This apparent curving is called the Coriolis effect. In the Northern Hemisphere it deflects moving air and water to the right of their path; in the Southern Hemisphere to the left. The result is that tropical storms in the Northern Hemisphere rotate counter-clockwise and those in the Southern Hemisphere rotate clockwise. It also helps drive the big trade-wind and ocean-current patterns of the globe.

the-darkest-skies-on-earth-where-the-mil.context_blurb: In the age of city lights, truly dark night skies have become one of the world's rarer sights.
